ethiopia.content: Ethiopia’s Strategic Recalibration Concurrent with Uganda’s Withdrawal from Somalia – HORN REVIEW Home Research and Analysis Ethiopia and the World Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Publications Horn Review Journal Articles Policy Briefs The Greater Horn: Monthly Strategic Brief Horn Review Magazine Weekly Geopolitical Report Research Paper Commentary Event Flagship Events Conferences Brainstorming Sessions Team About Us Contact Us Search Home Research and Analysis Ethiopia and the World Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Publications Horn Review Journal Articles Policy Briefs The Greater Horn: Monthly Strategic Brief Horn Review Magazine Weekly Geopolitical Report Research Paper Commentary Event Flagship Events Conferences Brainstorming Sessions Team About Us Contact Us 2026-11-25 Ethiopia’s Strategic Recalibration Concurrent with Uganda’s Withdrawal from Somalia 0 Comments Uganda’s phased withdrawal from Somalia announced in late October 2026 and set for completion by the end of 2027 shows a structural shift in the Horn of Africa’s security. For nearly two decades Ugandan forces have formed a central pillar of the African Union’s efforts in the country, first under AMISOM and later under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia. Their departure which includes both bilateral contingents and those serving under the AU framework creates an immediate security space at a moment of acute political fragmentation in Mogadishu. For Ethiopia this is a clarifying moment that requires disciplined recalibration of military posture, alliance order and the defense of core national interests along the shared border. Uganda has long secured sensitive installations in and around Mogadishu including the presidential palace and the international airport. Its drawdown from positions in Lower Shabelle and related sectors removes a physical shield just as Somalia’s federal government confronts an unresolved political crisis. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s term expired in May 2026 and disagreements over electoral modalities have deepened tensions between the federal center and opposition actors as well as with several regional administrations. Into this space Al Shabaab stands to regain operational freedom along key approaches to the capital. Somali national forces still consolidating capacity are not yet positioned to fill the gap fully or rapidly. Mogadishu’s most probable response is heavier reliance on Turkish air and drone capabilities together with contributions from other partners including Egyptian forces operating under or alongside the AUSSOM framework. Turkey has invested substantially in Somalia through training facilities, infrastructure and hydrocarbon exploration. Reports indicate prospective resources in Somali offshore blocks with estimates of substantial reserves under active survey and drilling arrangements. Egypt’s involvement while framed as stabilization support is viewed by administrations in Puntland, Jubaland and South West State as an external presence that risks aggravating internal political fault lines. The resulting activities could intensify centrifugal pressures rather than contain them. Parallel constraints affect the broader mission with AUSSOM’s logistics backbone has facing uncertainty linked to decisions on United Nations Support Office in Somalia funding. Earlier notifications pointed toward reduced or terminated support around the end of 2026 with subsequent adjustments extending limited windows. Without reliable sustainment of fuel, medical services, transport and related enablers the operational viability of the roughly 12,000 strong mission becomes constrained. Continuing large scale Ethiopian deployments under a framework whose long term financing remains unresolved would present an inefficient use of national resources. A more coherent Ethiopian approach centers on two complementary tracks. The first is a measured reduction of force levels under AUSSOM accompanied by the consolidation of a resilient bilateral defense zone along the Ethiopian and Somali border. This zone extending approximately 100 to 150 kilometers inside Somali territory from the Dollo Ado area toward Ferfer and encompassing key localities in Gedo, Bakool and the approaches to Baidoa would serve multiple purposes. It would deny Al Shabaab the ability to use the borderlands as a staging ground for cross border operations. It would establish a clear geographic buffer that limits the westward projection of any external forces toward Ethiopian territory. And it would enable Ethiopia to shape security outcomes in southern Somalia from a position of geographic advantage rather than through open ended commitment to a financially strained multilateral mission. The second track involves deeper, direct security and economic engagement with regional administrations that share practical interests in containing Al Shabaab and managing the risks of excessive centralization. South West State, Jubaland and Puntland have demonstrated both capacity and willingness to function as autonomous partners on security matters. Strengthening these relationships reduces the leverage that any single federal configuration in Mogadishu might attempt to exercise and anchors Ethiopian influence in durable local realities. Uganda’s reported reorientation toward closer ties with Abu Dhabi adds a further diplomatic opening. Kampala’s evolving external partnerships create space for practical coordination among Ethiopia, Uganda and the United Arab Emirates on intelligence sharing, logistics and maritime access. The UAE’s established positions in Berbera and Bossaso offer complementary depth that can reinforce landward security arrangements. Such coordination need not take the form of a rigid alliance it can function as a flexible mechanism among actors with converging interests in regional stability and the prevention of exclusive spheres of influence. Ankara’s hydrocarbon exploration and infrastructure projects depend on a baseline of security that has historically benefited from broader regional military contributions. As Ethiopian forces consolidate closer to the border and reduce exposure in central Somalia the security environment around key assets will adjust. This creates natural incentives for dialogue. Turkey has every reason to seek predictable arrangements that protect its interests and Ethiopia is well placed to engage on the basis of mutual recognition of security requirements rather than open ended subsidy of external political preferences. The central error to avoid is the continued commitment of Ethiopian manpower and resources to sustain a political and security order in Mogadishu that yields diminishing returns for national defense while serving the strategic math of others. Parking forces under an AUSSOM framework whose sustainment is uncertain would constitute precisely such a misallocation. The alternative consolidating a defensible cross border zone cultivating practical partnerships with regional administrations and leveraging Ethiopia’s indispensable geographic and military position is not disengagement. It is the reassertion of agency. Uganda’s departure is frequently described as a loss for the African Union mission. For Ethiopia it is more accurately understood as a moment of clarity. The era of open ended subsidized security provision is drawing to a close. What replaces it will be shaped by those actors prepared to define their interests with precision defend them with credible capacity and negotiate from positions of strength. Ethiopia possesses the geography, the military capability and the historical stake required to influence that outcome. Acting with discipline and focus on national security priorities will determine whether the transition strengthens or erodes Ethiopia’s long term position in the Horn. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia is undergoing a strategic recalibration in response to Uganda's planned withdrawal from Somalia, which is set to conclude by the end of 2027. Uganda has been a crucial player in the African Union's military efforts in Somalia for nearly two decades, and its exit creates a security vacuum amid political instability in Mogadishu. This situation presents Ethiopia with an opportunity to reassess its military posture and alliances, particularly along its border with Somalia. The Ethiopian strategy involves reducing its forces under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission (AUSSOM) while establishing a defensive zone within Somalia to counter Al Shabaab and limit external influences. Additionally, Ethiopia aims to strengthen ties with regional administrations like South West State and Jubaland, fostering local partnerships to enhance security. Uganda's shift towards closer relations with the UAE may also facilitate regional coordination on security matters. Ethiopia's ability to navigate this transition effectively will be crucial for its long-term stability and influence in the Horn of Africa.

ethiopia.title: The Containment Logic of Littoral Exclusivity and the Paradox of Red Sea Security - horn review
ethiopia.content: The Containment Logic of Littoral Exclusivity and the Paradox of Red Sea Security – HORN REVIEW Home Research and Analysis Ethiopia and the World Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Publications Horn Review Journal Articles Policy Briefs The Greater Horn: Monthly Strategic Brief Horn Review Magazine Weekly Geopolitical Report Research Paper Commentary Event Flagship Events Conferences Brainstorming Sessions Team About Us Contact Us Search Home Research and Analysis Ethiopia and the World Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Publications Horn Review Journal Articles Policy Briefs The Greater Horn: Monthly Strategic Brief Horn Review Magazine Weekly Geopolitical Report Research Paper Commentary Event Flagship Events Conferences Brainstorming Sessions Team About Us Contact Us 2026-11-25 The Containment Logic of Littoral Exclusivity and the Paradox of Red Sea Security 0 Comments In various times, states seeking to limit the power, options or rise of a neighbor or rival have repeatedly used a various set of tools. Their employed mechanisms include constraining the target’s strategic space, preserve its dependencies, deny it independent capacity in key domains and shape the regional environment so that its growth and influence remains manageable. In order to do that, that state or coalition establishes an approach centered on a particular domain—such as a sea, a river basin, or a security architecture—asserting that these spaces belong exclusively to a defined category of states (littoral states, downstream states, or historical custodians). This approach is then used to render that country’s initiatives unlawful, strip them of legitimacy, and portray them as violations of the regional order. Egypt’s engagement with the Horn of Africa increasingly reflects this pattern, as it seeks to shape the political and security conditions surrounding the region. Particularly following the deterioration of relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea and Ethiopia’s renewed pursuit of maritime access, Egypt began to more actively advance the notion of littoral exclusivity, which gradually evolved and intersected with other regional domains. Classic containment aimed to restrict the expansion of a rival power. Littoral exclusivity does something similar by using control of the coastal interface and chokepoints to hem in a neighboring continental or landlocked power’s reach, trade options, and naval aspirations. In this sense, littoral exclusivity means asserting that only states with a coastline on a Red Sea may have a say in its security, access arrangements and political frameworks. When applied selectively against a proximate, dependent, non-littoral power and when merged with other mechanisms of influence building surrounding the country, it becomes containment. The objective of this move is to restrict Ethiopia’s strategic options, economic security, alliance choices and ability to project influence, while aiming to preserve the dominant littoral state’s regional primacy. Instead of confronting Ethiopia only bilaterally, Egypt has worked to rally support and expand its orbit of influence by doubling down on military, diplomatic, and economic ties with the states that surround it. Defense protocols, troop deployments, port access arrangements, and political alignment create an arc of influence. Egypt’s forward positioning in Somalia and Sudan illustrates its efforts to limit Ethiopia’s freedom of action on multiple flanks. Any efforts by Ethiopia to secure port access—including the 2024 memorandum of understanding with Somaliland that envisioned port facilities and possible naval presence—and a greater voice in Red Sea affairs are met with joint statements rejecting non-littoral involvement. At summits such as the New Alamein meeting of Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia, and in bilateral statements with Eritrea, Egyptian officials have insisted that Red Sea security belongs solely to coastal states. Within this picture, Somalia tends to occupy a distinct position, as it is the only member who still maintain a functional (if strained) diplomatic relation with Ethiopia. On various occasions, its president has expressed its support for Ethiopia’s sea access and in fact, indicated that it is open to facilitating it. Yet its actions suggest otherwise, given its political and strategic alignment with Egypt’s regional strategy. Another tool Egypt employs is issue linkage, whereby pressure in one domain is deliberately connected to another, making concessions or restraint in one area conditional on relief in the other. For instance, linking the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) dispute with Ethiopia’s pursuit of maritime access, while bringing additional factors into the equation, aims to multiply the points of leverage against Ethiopia. The exclusivity doctrine sits alongside Egypt’s long-standing opposition to the GERD. Earlier this year, Egypt was reportedly prepared to support Ethiopia’s commercial access to the Red Sea if Addis Ababa showed flexibility on the Nile dispute. Although Cairo later denied the report, the report may suggest an attempt to test the waters by assessing Ethiopia’s willingness to link its maritime ambitions with concessions over the GERD. It also points to Egypt’s interest in exploring additional bargaining leverage by bringing the two issues into the same diplomatic equation. Egypt has also doubled down on establishing ties with Ethiopia’s immediate neighbors as another mechanism to keep Ethiopia off guard. Egypt initially pursued this approach with Nile riparian states to secure their support for its position on the Nile dispute. However, its efforts appear not to have been productive, given its failure to stop the GERD, the ratification of the CFA, and the apparent alignment of most riparian states with Ethiopia’s position. Afterwards, as the two issues became increasingly interconnected, Egypt began to strengthen its relations with Ethiopia’s immediate neighbors and capitalize on any friction between Ethiopia and its neighbors. Besides, this would collectively help reduce Ethiopia’s strategic depth and options. Various factors have contributed to the sharpening of Egypt’s regional activities, including the Sudanese civil war and Ethiopia’s MoU with Somaliland. Such an encirclement strategy could help Egypt constrain Ethiopia’s regional influence, monitor its affairs and relations with neighboring countries closely, and its strategic options along a vital shared waterway. This exclusivity appears to be weaponized in the service of regional rivalries, in contrast to the practical realities of the Red Sea. Various extra-regional powers maintain naval task forces, military bases, or regular patrols in the region to protect the security of the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb. Meanwhile, on the other side of the waterway, the military confrontation involving the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has contributed to the region’s insecurity. This insecurity itself undercuts rigid exclusivity, particularly in light of Saudi Arabia’s recent pragmatic initiatives. Recognizing the need for more inclusive arrangements, Riyadh invited a diverse coalition of Arab, African, and Asian states, including non-littoral countries, to discuss maritime security. A strict “only littorals decide” principle overlooks the reality that the Red Sea functions as a lifeline extending well beyond the coastal states and that rigid exclusivity is incompatible with the region’s actual interdependence. Absolute claims that only coastal states decide have frequently been limited or overridden when the vital interests of non-littoral or highly dependent states, freedom of navigation, or regional interdependence are at stake. The international response to piracy off the Somali coast is particularly relevant to the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. Following the escalation of piracy in 2008, the United Nations Security Council adopted Resolution 1816 . The resolution authorized states cooperating with Somalia’s Transitional Federal Government to enter Somali territorial waters and use necessary means to repress piracy, subject to the resolution’s conditions. The decision reflected the recognition that piracy off Somalia was not simply a coastal security problem. It threatened international shipping, humanitarian deliveries, and commercial maritime routes. The international response subsequently involved naval deployments by the European Union, NATO, China, India, and other states. The recent resurgence of piracy in the region reinforces the point that maritime security in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden cannot be treated as the exclusive concern of littoral states, given its direct implications for international shipping and the security interests of states dependent on these waterways. All these indicate that when the interests of regional countries are deeply implicated—especially as the security of the region continues to deteriorate—their participation in addressing these challenges becomes essential. Ethiopia has contributed to counterterrorism efforts in Somalia for decades. Its role in peace support operations and the fight against al-Shabaab has made it an important actor in regional security. Ethiopia’s security environment is closely intertwined with developments in the Red Sea, particularly given the threats posed by al-Shabaab, domestic insurgent groups, and maritime insecurity. Meanwhile, the reported links between the Houthis and al-Shabaab across the Gulf of Aden add another layer of concern, potentially creating new security risks for Ethiopia and the wider Horn of Africa. Absolute claims of littoral exclusivity have historically proven difficult to sustain when the vital interests of non-littoral states, freedom of navigation, or regional interdependence are at stake, as the international response to piracy and the sustained presence of extra-regional naval forces have already shown. In the current Red Sea setting, the rigid application of this doctrine risks deepening regional polarization, narrowing diplomatic space, and raising the costs of any future arrangement. Moreover, Egypt’s reported willingness to consider supporting Ethiopia’s commercial sea access in exchange for flexibility on the GERD reveals the instrumental nature of the exclusivity rhetoric and risks leaving the neighbors who echoed Cairo’s position looking as if they were used to advance a bargaining strategy that was never absolute. ethiopia.summary: The article discusses Egypt's strategy of "littoral exclusivity" in the Red Sea, which aims to limit Ethiopia's influence and access to maritime resources. This approach involves asserting that only coastal states can dictate security and political frameworks in the region, effectively sidelining landlocked Ethiopia. Egypt's efforts to contain Ethiopia include strengthening military, diplomatic, and economic ties with neighboring states like Sudan and Somalia, while simultaneously opposing Ethiopia's maritime ambitions and linking them to disputes over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD). The article highlights the paradox of this exclusivity, as it contradicts the reality of regional interdependence and the involvement of non-littoral states in ensuring maritime security. The presence of international naval forces and the historical challenges of piracy further complicate the notion that only littoral states should govern Red Sea security. Ultimately, the rigid application of this doctrine risks exacerbating regional tensions and undermining collaborative security efforts.

ethiopia.title: From Catalyst for Change to Source of Uncertainty - the Power--and Peril--of the Political Disrupter
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: From Catalyst for Change to Source of Uncertainty - the Power--and Peril--of the Political Disrupter - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: From Catalyst for Change to Source of Uncertainty - the Power--and Peril--of the Political Disrupter 25 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) opinion Addis Abeba — In politics, the most consequential figure is not always the person holding public office or leading a political party. Sometimes influence belongs to an individual who stands just outside the formal structure: the broadcaster who can mobilize a crowd, the activist who can unsettle an established order, the insider who can fracture a coalition, or the political entrepreneur who thrives on keeping the landscape in perpetual motion. Such a figure may be described as a political disrupter. Disruption, however, is not inherently destructive. Political progress often begins when someone challenges a complacent establishment, exposes entrenched injustice, or forces a reluctant society to confront questions it has long avoided. Yet the same capacity to unsettle can be turned against the very movement that once benefited from it. A disrupter can become a catalyst for reform--or a spoiler who leaves political forces weaker, more divided, and less capable of producing change. The distinction lies not simply in whom the disrupter criticizes but in the purpose, consistency, methods, and destination of the disruption. Does the intervention open a path toward a more accountable political order, or does it merely deepen confusion and mistrust? Does it build institutions and common ground, or does it leave others to pick up the pieces? Understanding the political disrupter Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn In Ethiopian politics, we have seen many political activists and commentators, as well as media influencers and actors. A political disrupter is an actor whose words, actions, networks, or strategic interventions significantly disturb established political relationships or institutions. Formal office is not a prerequisite; influence can be exercised through public credibility, access to information, organizational networks, identity-based mobilization, or the ability to shape the political narrative. The term should not be confused with ordinary dissent. In a democracy, criticism, protest, opposition, and the exposure of government failure are legitimate and often indispensable. A government that labels every critic a disrupter is likely attempting to delegitimize scrutiny. Equally, a political movement that treats every internal question as betrayal may be protecting its leadership from accountability rather than protecting its cause. The more useful question is whether disruption is constructive, accountable, and directed toward a coherent political outcome--or whether it is opportunistic, destabilizing, and indifferent to the consequences. Different faces of political disruption Political disruption can take several forms, depending on the actor's intentions and objectives. It can be constructive, as when change agents challenge corruption, authoritarianism, and institutional failure to advance reform and accountability. Conversely, political spoilers undermine negotiations and alliances by exploiting mistrust and deepening divisions without offering credible alternatives. More dangerously, agents provocateurs incite actions that expose others to repression or internal collapse, while controlled opposition involves actors secretly manipulated or tolerated by those in power to weaken genuine dissent--a serious allegation that requires compelling evidence. Political entrepreneurs and wedge-makers, meanwhile, exploit existing rivalries and instability to maintain influence, often at the expense of collective progress. Ultimately, the distinction is whether disruption creates a pathway to meaningful reform or merely perpetuates division, uncertainty, and instability. Disruption: Engineered, exploited, or self-generated? Political disruption can arise in at least three ways. It may be deliberately engineered by an actor seeking to weaken a rival; it may be opportunistically exploited by a political force that did not create the crisis; or it may be self-generated through impulsive rhetoric, inconsistent positioning, personal ambition, or an inability to distinguish tactical advantage from strategic purpose. These categories must not be conflated. Evidence of coordination is required before describing an individual as planted, controlled, or acting on behalf of another power. But the absence of proof of external direction does not prevent a fair assessment of political consequences. An actor can destabilize a movement without intending to do so, just as a government can benefit from an opposition figure's intervention without having orchestrated it. In politics, intention matters; consequences matter too." In politics, intention matters; consequences matter too. A serious analysis examines both, while resisting the temptation to turn suspicion into fact. Ethiopia: When influence outruns political institutions Ethiopia's political landscape provides fertile ground for the rise of unconventional political actors. Weak institutional trust, armed conflict, contested national identity, ethnic and regional grievances, and a fragmented opposition environment create openings for individuals who can command attention beyond formal party structures. In such circumstances, media influence and the ability to mobilize supporters may carry more immediate weight than membership in a political organization. The danger is that political influence can become detached from institutional responsibility. A figure may shape public expectations, encourage mobilization, criticize alliances, or redirect debate without being accountable for the practical consequences. When a political movement lacks a clear program and credible institutions, personalities can become substitutes for strategy--and political theater can displace political work. Jawar Mohammed: From mobilisation to political enigma Jawar Mohammed's political trajectory illustrates why the role of a disrupter deserves careful examination. He became a prominent Oromo political voice through the Oromia Media Network and his influence during the 2014-2018 protest movement. Human Rights Watch described him as instrumental in the movement that helped bring Abiy Ahmed to power and noted his significant following among Oromo communities, including youth activists associated with Qeerroo. That influence, however, should not be mistaken for the sole command of a broad movement whose mobilisation involved many local actors and networks. During the early transition after Abiy took office, Jawar's public influence placed him close to the center of Ethiopia's political transformation. His later falling-out with the prime minister, imprisonment, and subsequent return to public political debate further complicated his position. His history cannot be reduced to a single label: he has at different times been a mobilizer, critic, political ally, adversary, and influential commentator. The more pressing question concerns the consistency and strategic direction of his recent interventions. In September 2026, following the announcement of the Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival by seven armed opposition groups, Jawar questioned the alliance's popularity among Oromos and challenged whether its members shared a political or tactical objective. Those are legitimate questions. Nevertheless, the group of seven alliance movements, despite their different histories, constituencies, and immediate grievances, have outlined how they strive for an interim transitional government that will include all, resolve internal disputes, and protect civilians. Dismissing the alliance simply because of its diversity or internal complexities risks undermining a broader aspiration that a significant number of Ethiopians share: the hope for a peaceful political transition and a more inclusive future. Nevertheless, criticism becomes politically consequential when it is not accompanied by a constructive alternative. If an influential figure rejects a coalition, the public is entitled to ask, "What alternative platform does he propose? What political forces should cooperate, on what principles, and toward what constitutional destination?" Without answers, criticism risks becoming an exercise in demolition without reconstruction. The recent violence around Moyale offers another important test of political framing. In an assessment I heard, Jawar characterized the confrontation primarily as a recurring dispute between the Garre and Borana communities over grazing land. The historical boundary and resource disputes between these communities are real and cannot be ignored. Yet the October 2026 escalation cannot be adequately understood through that lens alone. Media outlets documented clashes beginning on 18 October after a dispute over the opening of a Somali regional administration office and the raising of a regional flag in a contested locality. The violence spread across several locations and involved Somali regional police, Oromia regional police, and local militias. According to reports , nearly 700,000 people have been displaced by the Moyale conflict along Ethiopia's border with Kenya. In a 7 November 2026 interview on the YouTube program My Journalism Toolkit , Jawar addressed the issue directly, stating, "So this conflict is not between Somalis and Oromos. It is not. There is no territorial dispute between Somalis and Oromos." His statement is important because it rejects a framing of the violence as a territorial contest between the two communities. Yet the absence of a formal territorial dispute between Somalis and Oromos does not, by itself, explain the administrative dispute, the involvement of regional security forces, or the displacement that followed. Those dimensions still require examination. The distinction is significant. A localized dispute may have historical roots in land, grazing, and boundaries; once regional security forces, competing administrations, and wider ethnic identities become involved, the conflict acquires a broader political and security dimension. To describe it only as "a familiar clan-level resource dispute" risks understating the escalation and its potential to spread. Oromo and Somali communities have longstanding social, cultural, and economic ties . Responsible political commentary should avoid language that hardens communal suspicion and should instead identify the institutional failures and political decisions that can turn a local dispute into a wider confrontation. Jawar's recent advocacy around Ethiopia's access to the sea raises a further question about strategic consistency. In October 2026, reports described a "Now or Never" campaign associated with him that urged military action against Eritrea to secure sea access. This position warrants scrutiny because the use of force carries enormous risks for Ethiopia and the wider Horn of Africa. It is also important to distinguish convergence on one policy objective from endorsement of the government's broader agenda. Taken together, these episodes do not establish that Jawar is a controlled opposition, an agent provocateur, or a deliberate instrument of the government. There is no basis here to make that claim. They do, however, raise a legitimate analytical question: has a figure once associated with mass political mobilisation become a political disrupter whose interventions increasingly unsettle opposition coordination without clarifying a viable alternative? That is a question about observable political conduct and consequences--not a verdict on hidden motives. How to recognise disruption without mistaking it for leadership Several questions can help distinguish constructive disruption from political sabotage or drift. Does the actor offer a coherent alternative after criticizing others? Are standards applied consistently to allies, opponents, and the government? Does the intervention widen the space for peaceful political participation or intensify polarization? Does it strengthen institutions and collective decision-making or make the political process dependent on one personality? And, crucially, is the actor prepared to accept responsibility for foreseeable consequences? A disrupter may be indispensable in opening a closed political system, but disruption alone cannot govern a country or sustain a movement." Leadership is not measured by the ability to command attention or unsettle rivals. It is measured by the capacity to convert influence into direction, disagreement into negotiation, and public frustration into a credible program. A disrupter may be indispensable in opening a closed political system, but disruption alone cannot govern a country or sustain a movement. There was a problem processing your submission. Please try again later. The cost of disruption without direction For Ethiopia, the stakes are particularly high. The country is already burdened by multiple armed conflicts, unresolved constitutional questions, displacement, economic pressure, and deep mistrust among political communities. In such a setting, political actors who amplify divisions without offering a pathway to reconciliation may unintentionally--or deliberately--make an already combustible environment more dangerous. Opposition movements also carry a responsibility to the public. Their task is not merely to oppose the incumbent government; they must demonstrate that they can build a more inclusive and accountable political order. Coalitions need shared principles, transparent decision-making, and credible civilian leadership. Critics who identify weaknesses in such coalitions can make a valuable contribution--but only if they help clarify what should replace them. The government, for its part, should not exploit opposition divisions as a substitute for addressing the grievances that fuel dissent. Nor should it dismiss criticism as sabotage. A healthy political environment requires space for disagreement, scrutiny, and peaceful competition. The same standards must apply to all political actors. Conclusion: Disruption must have destination The political disrupter is a paradoxical figure: capable of breaking political deadlock, yet equally capable of deepening it. The same influence that can awaken a society may also fracture its alliances. The same voice that once mobilized people for change may later become a source of uncertainty if it cannot articulate a consistent political destination. Ethiopia does not need silence from its critics. It needs criticism that illuminates rather than obscures, opposition that proposes rather than merely denounces, and leaders who understand that political influence carries public responsibility. The decisive question is not whether a figure disrupts the political order, but what that disruption is intended to build. Disruption without direction can become another form of political paralysis. Influence without accountability can become a liability. And opposition without a credible alternative can leave a nation trapped between the order it rejects and the future it cannot define. ethiopia.summary: In Ethiopia, political disrupters—individuals who influence politics from outside formal structures—play a complex role in shaping the political landscape. These figures can catalyze change by challenging entrenched injustices or destabilize movements by deepening divisions. The distinction between constructive disruption and destructive interference hinges on the intentions and outcomes of their actions. For instance, Jawar Mohammed, a prominent Oromo political voice, exemplifies this duality. Initially instrumental in mobilizing support during protests, his later criticisms of political alliances raise questions about his strategic direction. Recent conflicts, such as the violence in Moyale, illustrate the risks of oversimplifying complex issues, as they involve broader political dynamics beyond local disputes. As Ethiopia navigates its political challenges, understanding the impact of disrupters like Jawar is crucial, as their influence can either foster accountability or perpetuate instability, highlighting the need for constructive alternatives in political discourse.

ethiopia.title: Sudan's Army-Aligned Government Rejects Abiy's Dialogue Call - RSF-Backed Administration Welcomes It
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Sudan's Army-Aligned Government Rejects Abiy's Dialogue Call - RSF-Backed Administration Welcomes It - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Sudan's Army-Aligned Government Rejects Abiy's Dialogue Call - RSF-Backed Administration Welcomes It 25 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Sudan's army-aligned government has rejected Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's invitation for an inclusive Sudanese dialogue hosted in Ethiopia, while a rival administration aligned with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has welcomed the initiative, highlighting divisions over Ethiopia's proposed role in efforts to end Sudan's war. The latest developments follow an announcement earlier this week by the Sudan Founding Alliance (Ta'asis), an alliance aligned with the RSF, that it had dispatched a senior delegation to Addis Abeba for talks with the five-party mediation mechanism comprising the African Union (AU), United Nations (UN), European Union (EU), Arab League, and Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD). The meeting, scheduled for Wednesday, November 25, at the African Union Commission headquarters, was intended to address procedural concerns previously raised by Ta'asis and discuss ways to advance the political process. The engagement was separate from Ethiopia's subsequent initiative to host a comprehensive Sudanese dialogue. On November 24, Abiy called on Sudanese military, political, and civilian actors to participate in an inclusive dialogue hosted and sponsored by Ethiopia, with the stated aim of ending the war, building national consensus, and paving the way for a national unity government. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Abiy said Ethiopia's initiative was not driven by a political agenda or an attempt to secure gains at the expense of any Sudanese party, but by concern for Sudan's future and the consequences of continued fighting. "The true winner should be Sudan and its people," Abiy said, warning that continued conflict would deepen the destruction of the country's institutions, history, diversity, and future. He said Ethiopia was prepared to stand "at the same distance as all parties" and provide a platform for dialogue based on openness, seriousness, and mutual respect, allowing Sudanese actors to reach solutions of their own accord. Abiy further said the proposed dialogue could lead to broader political agreements, including the formation of a national unity government, restoration of state institutions, reconstruction, and a lasting peace. He stressed that Sudan's future must be determined by Sudanese themselves, arguing that imposed solutions could not deliver sustainable peace. On November 24, the RSF-aligned Transitional Peace Government welcomed the invitation and expressed readiness to engage positively with it. In a statement issued by Minister of Information and government spokesperson Khalid Ahmed Dana, the administration praised Ethiopia's solidarity with Sudan and its stated commitment to the country's unity, sovereignty, and stability. The statement reaffirmed the administration's determination to pursue "comprehensive, just, and sustainable peace," describing the invitation as an opportunity to help end the war and address its underlying causes. However, on Wednesday, November 25, Sudan's army-aligned government formally rejected the Ethiopian initiative, arguing that Ethiopia could not serve as a neutral host or facilitator amid allegations that it supports the RSF. In a statement carried by the state-run Sudan News Agency (SUNA), the government accused Ethiopia of allowing RSF-linked drone operations from its territory to strike targets inside Sudan. It called for an independent investigation into the allegations, reserved the right to take diplomatic and legal measures, and urged regional and international actors to exclude Ethiopia from any arrangements to host or facilitate Sudanese dialogue. The government insisted that the venue, agenda, and facilitator for any peace process should be determined by Sudanese parties through consensus. Relations between Addis Abeba and Sudan's army-aligned authorities have been staidly deteriorating following accusations that Ethiopia us providing the RSF with logistical support , training facilities, and access to territory for drone operations . Ethiopia has consistently denied the allegations, while counteraccusing Sudan of supporting armed groups operating against the Ethiopian government. Diplomatic tensions escalated earlier this month, with Ethiopia closing Sudan's consulate in Assosa and expelling Sudanese diplomats, followed by Sudan's closure of Ethiopia's consulate in Gedaref and the expulsion of its staff. This week marked another sharp turn in the tensions after drone attacks on Khartoum on Sunday, November 22 damaged residential properties and a UN facility. The strikes drew condemnation from Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Egypt, Kuwait, Jordan, the United States, and the United Nations, with Washington calling for an end to the flow of foreign-supplied drones into Sudan. A Sudanese army source told the media that the drones had been launched from Bahir Dar airport in Ethiopia's Amhara region, describing the attack as a continuation of what it called Ethiopian aggression against Sudanese territory. ethiopia.summary: Sudan's army-aligned government has rejected Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's call for an inclusive dialogue aimed at resolving the ongoing conflict in Sudan. In contrast, a rival administration aligned with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has welcomed the initiative, indicating a split in Sudanese factions regarding Ethiopia's role in peace efforts. Abiy's proposal, made on November 24, emphasized the need for a dialogue free from political agendas, aiming to foster national consensus and establish a unity government. However, the army-aligned government accused Ethiopia of bias, alleging it supports the RSF and has facilitated drone operations against Sudan. This rejection comes amid escalating diplomatic tensions, including mutual consulate closures and accusations of foreign drone strikes. The RSF-aligned Transitional Peace Government expressed readiness to engage with Ethiopia's initiative, viewing it as a chance to address the war's root causes and pursue sustainable peace. The situation remains complex, with ongoing allegations and deteriorating relations between Sudan and Ethiopia. (157 words)

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Vows Direct Role in Shaping Red Sea Security Architecture, Maritime Governance
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Vows Direct Role in Shaping Red Sea Security Architecture, Maritime Governance - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia Vows Direct Role in Shaping Red Sea Security Architecture, Maritime Governance 25 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Red Sea security is an integral part of Ethiopia's national security, and the country will continue to play a direct and constructive role in regional maritime governance, Chief of Staff at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ambassador Adam Tesfaye, said. The two-day fifth edition of the Horn Dialogue Series is underway in Addis Ababa under the theme: "Re-collaborating Regionalism in the Horn of Africa: Building Strategic Trust, Regional Agency, and Cooperative Interdependence." Opening the dialogue series, Ambassador Adam described the Horn Dialogue Series as an important platform that brings together scholars, diplomats, and other stakeholders to exchange views on pressing regional issues and explore solutions to shared challenges. He pointed out that the Horn of Africa is among the world's most strategically significant regions, with considerable potential for economic growth, supported by its geographical proximity and strong economic and social ties among countries in the region. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn However, he said the region continues to face multiple challenges. The ambassador pointed out that this geopolitically significant part of the world continues to face multiple challenges, including interstate tensions, internal conflicts, competing national priorities, differing security perceptions, and shifting regional alliances. According to him, these challenges cannot be addressed through individual efforts, stressing the need for coordinated regional responses to economic, social, traditional, transnational, and maritime security concerns. He stated that regional integration remains essential to addressing the region's multifaceted challenges, although translating shared interests in peace, stability, economic development, and connectivity into concrete collective action remains a major challenge. Adam reaffirmed Ethiopia's commitment to regional and continental integration. He further noted that the government firmly believes economic integration serves the best interests of the peoples of the region. He also emphasized Ethiopia's efforts to strengthen regional connectivity through investments in transport and energy infrastructure, as well as its active engagement in regional peace and security initiatives within the frameworks of the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the African Union (AU), and the United Nations (UN). Addressing maritime security, Ambassador Adam underscored the strategic importance of the Red Sea to regional stability, reiterating that its security is directly linked to Ethiopia's national security. In this regard, Ethiopia will continue to play a direct and constructive role in Red Sea governance while pursuing secure and reliable access to the sea through peaceful dialogue, diplomacy, international law, and mutual benefit, he noted. "We strongly believe that Red Sea security plays a pivotal role in the security of our region and is an integral part of Ethiopia's national security," he said. He reiterated that Ethiopia would continue to play a direct and constructive role in Red Sea governance, stressing that such an approach would contribute to advancing peace, prosperity, and strategic cooperation across the region. For his part, Gizachew Asrat, Chief of Staff at the Institute of Foreign Affairs, highlighted the region's critical position linking the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, and the Indian Ocean. He stressed that persistent trust deficits and fragmented cooperation have prevented Horn nations from fully capitalizing on their geographical proximity. "The central question is how we can transform the Horn of Africa from a region characterized by geopolitical competition into one defined by shared interests and economic complementarities," Gizachew said. Paul-Simon Handy, Regional Director for East Africa and Representative to the AU at the Institute for Security Studies (ISS), traced the evolution of the dialogue series since its inception in Djibouti in 2022, noting that the fifth edition convenes at a critical juncture marked by renewed regional instability. Handy explained that this year's panels are structured around three core pillars: fostering strategic trust among neighbors with competing interests, asserting regional agency so external actors do not dictate the Horn's security agenda, and advancing "cooperative interdependence" even when political relations remain strained. Jan-Ole Voss, Director of the Konrad Adenauer Stiftung (KAS) Regional Programme Security Dialogue for East Africa, underscored that sustainable solutions must be locally driven rather than externally imposed. "The future of the Horn will ultimately be decided and determined by the countries and peoples of the region," Voss said, noting that recalibrating regionalism means building upon existing AU and IGAD frameworks rather than replacing them. Reaffirming Germany and the European Union's support for multilateral dialogue in the region, he added that trust cannot be built overnight but develops gradually through transparency, predictability, and sustained engagement. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia has reaffirmed its commitment to playing a direct role in shaping the security architecture and maritime governance of the Red Sea, which it considers integral to its national security. During the fifth edition of the Horn Dialogue Series in Addis Ababa, Ambassador Adam Tesfaye emphasized the importance of regional cooperation to address challenges such as interstate tensions and internal conflicts. He highlighted the strategic significance of the Horn of Africa, advocating for coordinated responses to economic, social, and security issues. Ethiopia aims to enhance regional connectivity through investments in infrastructure and active participation in peace initiatives under the frameworks of IGAD, AU, and UN. The dialogue series aims to foster strategic trust and cooperative interdependence among Horn nations, with experts stressing the need for locally driven solutions to ensure sustainable regional stability. The discussions reflect a critical juncture for the region, marked by renewed instability and the necessity for collaborative efforts to transform geopolitical competition into shared economic interests. ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Showcases Africa's Potential Through Tangible Milestones in Health Sector
ethiopia.content: Africa: Ethiopia Showcases Africa's Potential Through Tangible Milestones in Health Sector - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: Ethiopia Showcases Africa's Potential Through Tangible Milestones in Health Sector 25 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Ethiopia is demonstrating Africa's capabilities and potential through tangible achievements and transformative progress in the healthcare sector, Minister of Health Dr. Mekdes Daba said. Speaking to ENA on the sidelines of the 5th International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA 2026), currently underway at the Addis International Convention Center with more than 30,000 participants from over 100 countries, Dr. Mekdes highlighted the strong multisectoral engagement and high-level participation at the event. She noted that, alongside health officials, more than 46 ministers representing finance, planning, agriculture, and environmental protection are also attending the conference. The Minister emphasized that conference delegates have had the opportunity to witness firsthand Ethiopia's impactful initiatives, proven best practices, and far-reaching transformations across other key development sectors. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn She explained that these achievements stand as tangible evidence of the nation's capacity to translate ambitions into concrete results, significantly strengthening international confidence in Africa's potential. Through this collaborative platform, which brings together government and non-governmental institutions, development partners, and the private sector, Ethiopia is also showcasing its scientific and technological advancements across multiple areas, Dr. Mekdes noted. In particular, participants have witnessed the country's pioneering work in artificial intelligence, digital health, primary healthcare, and medical referral systems. The practical application of the Electronic Community Health Information System (eCHIS), an innovative digital platform that enables Health Extension Workers to efficiently monitor, track, and manage community health services, was also among the advancements showcased to delegates. As a result, several countries have expressed keen interest in adopting Ethiopia's healthcare models and digital solutions, creating new opportunities for knowledge exchange, cooperation, and the sharing of best practices. Addressing the evolving dynamics of global health governance, the Minister highlighted Ethiopia's strategic use of health diplomacy to strengthen Africa's voice, influence, and standing on the international stage. She affirmed that the conference will help translate the vision of Africa's health sovereignty into concrete actions and meaningful resolutions. The agreement was reached during a meeting today between Ethiopia's Ambassador to Pakistan, Oumer Hussein, and Pakistan's Federal Secretary for Defence, Lt. Gen. (R) Muhammad Ali, in Rawalpindi, Pakistan. The two sides discussed issues of mutual interest, including regional peace and security, as well as opportunities to expand cooperation in defence and aviation. Ambassador Oumer reaffirmed Ethiopia's commitment to working closely with the Pakistani government to strengthen bilateral relations through expanded cooperation in trade, investment, defence, aviation, tourism, and culture. For his part, Federal Secretary Muhammad Ali assured the Ethiopian Ambassador of his full support in advancing the partnership between the two countries under Pakistan's "Look Africa" and "Engage Africa" policies. ethiopia.title: Obasanjo to Chair Sasakawa Africa Association's 40th Anniversary Symposium in Addis Ababa
ethiopia.content: Africa: Obasanjo to Chair Sasakawa Africa Association's 40th Anniversary Symposium in Addis Ababa - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: Obasanjo to Chair Sasakawa Africa Association's 40th Anniversary Symposium in Addis Ababa 25 November 2026 Nile Post (Kampala) By Kenneth Kazibwe Former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo is set to chair the Sasakawa Africa Association's (SAA) 40th anniversary symposium scheduled for December 1-2, 2026, in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, bringing together African leaders, policymakers, agricultural experts and development partners to discuss the future of the continent's food and nutrition security. The two-day symposium, organised by SAA with longstanding support from The Nippon Foundation, will reflect on four decades of agricultural transformation while exploring innovative strategies and partnerships to strengthen Africa's agrifood systems. Held under the theme "Reimagining Africa's Food and Nutrition Security," the gathering will bring together regional leaders, farmers, researchers, policymakers, private-sector representatives and development partners to examine progress made in agricultural development and identify opportunities for building resilient and sustainable food systems. Obasanjo, a former member of the SAA Board, will chair the symposium, drawing on his longstanding advocacy for agricultural development and agribusiness as key drivers of economic growth, employment creation and food security. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn In an earlier interview with SAA, the former Nigerian leader underscored the importance of food security to national stability, describing it as a fundamental pillar of security and development. "For any country in Africa, food security is next to personal security," Obasanjo said. He also highlighted the importance of developing agribusiness across the entire agricultural value chain, arguing that its contribution extends beyond farming and food production to include land preparation, agricultural equipment, processing, distribution and delivery of food to consumers. According to Obasanjo, strengthening agribusiness presents significant opportunities for employment creation, wealth generation and improved food and nutrition security across Africa. The symposium will feature high-level policy discussions and practical exchanges focusing on agricultural extension, climate resilience, food and nutrition security, investment, innovation and the development of inclusive agricultural value chains. Established in 1986 through the shared vision of Japanese philanthropist Ryoichi Sasakawa, Nobel Peace Prize laureate Dr Norman E. Borlaug and former United States President Jimmy Carter, SAA has spent four decades supporting agricultural development and improving the livelihoods of smallholder farmers across Africa. The organisation has operated in 17 African countries, working to strengthen agricultural extension systems, promote improved farming practices and connect farmers and other agricultural value-chain actors to knowledge, technologies and markets. A key component of its work is the Sasakawa Africa Fund for Extension Education (SAFE), which partners with African universities and agricultural colleges to develop practical, demand-driven degree and diploma programmes for mid-career agricultural extension professionals. SAFE currently operates in Ethiopia, Mali, Nigeria and Uganda, with support from The Nippon Foundation, alongside other development partners, donors and collaborating institutions. The 40th anniversary symposium will also showcase success stories from SAA's country programmes, lessons from its agricultural interventions and experiences of young agrifood entrepreneurs, highlighting opportunities to expand the participation of the next generation in Africa's agricultural transformation. A commemorative exhibition titled "40 Years of Walking with the Farmer" will showcase the organisation's four-decade journey through farmer success stories, agricultural innovations and milestones achieved across its country programmes. Participants will also review SAA's 2026-2030 Strategic Plan, which outlines the organisation's priorities for the coming years. The strategy focuses on building climate-resilient and sustainable agrifood systems, expanding inclusive markets and agribusiness opportunities, and advancing access to safe, adequate and nutritious food. The anniversary gathering is expected to provide an opportunity for African agricultural stakeholders and international development partners to reflect on lessons from the past four decades while strengthening collaboration towards a more productive, inclusive and food-secure continent. The symposium and associated technical sessions will be held physically in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, from December 1 to 2, 2026. Read the original article on Nile Post . Offers to Host Inclusive Dialogue to End Sudan’s War The Ethiopian prime minister reaffirmed his country's support for Sudan's unity, territorial integrity and stability, saying peace in Sudan was closely linked to security across the Horn of Africa. G Garowe Online 25 Nov 2026 · 15:04 · 2 min read Abiy Ahmed, the prime minister of Ethiopia ADDIS ABABA, Ethiopia — Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has invited Sudan’s military, political and civilian groups to participate in an inclusive national dialogue hosted and facilitated by Ethiopia, as his government seeks to help end the war that has devastated the neighboring country. In a statement issued in Arabic, Abiy said Ethiopia was proposing a new initiative to bring together all Sudanese parties for comprehensive talks aimed at ending hostilities and establishing a path toward lasting peace. “At this critical historical juncture, the Ethiopian government is putting forward a sincere and genuine initiative calling on all Sudanese parties, across their military, political, and civilian components, to participate in a comprehensive and open Sudanese dialogue to be hosted and facilitated by Ethiopia,” he said. Abiy described the conflict, which erupted on April 15, 2023, as more than a political and security crisis, saying it had become a humanitarian tragedy with consequences extending beyond Sudan’s borders and threatening stability across the region. He said Ethiopia's historical, cultural and people-to-people ties with Sudan made the conflict particularly concerning for Ethiopians, describing the Sudanese as a brotherly people whose suffering resonated deeply with their neighbors. The Ethiopian prime minister reaffirmed his country's support for Sudan's unity, territorial integrity and stability, saying peace in Sudan was closely linked to security across the Horn of Africa. Abiy also recalled Ethiopia's diplomatic involvement during Sudan's political transition in 2019, when Addis Ababa sought to bring civilian and military leaders closer together and support efforts toward civilian rule. He said the latest initiative was intended to provide a neutral and inclusive platform where Sudanese stakeholders could address their differences through dialogue and political consensus. The proposed talks would seek to end the fighting, bridge political and military divisions and establish arrangements for a broader political transition, including the formation of a national unity government with wide support. Abiy stressed that Ethiopia's initiative was not designed to advance a particular political agenda or favor any of the parties involved in the conflict. He said his government was prepared to maintain equal distance from all sides and facilitate credible and respectful discussions. He added that Sudanese people must determine their country's future through their own national will, warning that solutions imposed from outside would not deliver sustainable peace. The war in Sudan has pitted the Sudanese army against the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, triggering a major humanitarian crisis and forcing millions of people from their homes. The conflict has also raised concerns among neighboring countries over regional security and the growing displacement of civilians. Abiy did not announce a date for the proposed dialogue or specify whether the Sudanese parties had accepted the invitation. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has proposed hosting an inclusive national dialogue to help end the ongoing war in Sudan, which has caused significant humanitarian crises and regional instability since its outbreak on April 15, 2023. In a statement, Abiy emphasized the importance of Sudan's unity and stability for the security of the Horn of Africa and called for participation from all Sudanese military, political, and civilian groups. He described the conflict as a humanitarian tragedy affecting not only Sudan but also its neighbors. The initiative aims to create a neutral platform for dialogue, allowing Sudanese stakeholders to address their differences and work towards a national unity government. Abiy assured that Ethiopia would remain impartial and that the future of Sudan should be determined by its people, warning against externally imposed solutions. No specific date for the dialogue has been announced, nor has there been confirmation of acceptance from the Sudanese parties.

somalia.content: Somalia dismisses security vacuum fears as Ugandan troops withdraw - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY Somalia dismisses security vacuum fears as Ugandan troops withdraw Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Sunday November 22, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somali federal government has dismissed concerns that the withdrawal of Ugandan troops could create a security vacuum, insisting that the Somali National Army is prepared to take over positions vacated by foreign forces. Speaking during a BBC Somali debate on Friday, Information Minister Abdifatah Qasim Mohamud said the government had spent recent years strengthening and training its armed forces, including soldiers who recently returned from military training abroad. He said Ugandan troops had already handed over some of their positions directly to Somali forces as part of the ongoing security transition. advertisements "We have no concerns that this will negatively impact the country's security situation or the areas vacated by these troops," Abdifatah said. The minister emphasized that foreign troops were deployed to Somalia for specific missions and limited periods, arguing that their departure should not be interpreted as evidence that Somalia lacks the military capacity to protect itself. He said Somalia's security could not remain permanently dependent on international peacekeeping forces and that the government was committed to assuming full responsibility for national security. His remarks follow Uganda's announcement earlier this month that it had begun withdrawing troops deployed under bilateral security arrangements with Somalia. The Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) said the withdrawal would be conducted in phases, with all Ugandan troops, including those serving under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), expected to leave by the end of 2027. Uganda has been one of the largest contributors to African Union peacekeeping operations in Somalia since 2007, with its forces playing a major role in securing Mogadishu and supporting military operations against al-Shabab. The planned withdrawal has raised concerns among some security officials and lawmakers about the readiness of Somali forces to assume responsibility for strategic locations previously protected by Ugandan troops. Abdifatah specifically challenged comments made by lawmaker Kooshin during a BBC Somali discussion, in which the MP reportedly warned that Somalia was not yet prepared to take full control of areas vacated by Ugandan peacekeepers. Kooshin argued that security in Mogadishu and parts of Lower Shabelle and Middle Shabelle remained dependent on African Union forces. Responding to the criticism, the information minister questioned whether areas that had previously fallen under al-Shabab control had been liberated exclusively by Somali troops or with the support of international peacekeepers. He maintained that the Somali National Army had played the leading role in liberating several areas from the militant group, citing military operations between Mogadishu and Harardhere as examples. Abdifatah said the federal government had made significant investments in military training and capacity-building over the past five years to prepare national forces for greater security responsibilities. However, concerns about the withdrawal have also been raised by international security officials. In a report earlier this month, Reuters cited an African Union communication warning that the departure of Ugandan forces could leave parts of Lower Shabelle vulnerable to attacks by al-Shabab. Somalia's State Minister for Foreign Affairs, Ali Mohamed Omar, also previously acknowledged that a sudden withdrawal could create security problems, although he said the situation was not immediately critical. The differing assessments reflect continued debate over Somalia's readiness to complete the security transition as African Union troop-contributing countries review their deployments and international funding remains uncertain. Al-Shabab, an al-Qaeda-linked militant group, continues to carry out attacks against Somali security forces and maintains a presence in parts of southern and central Somalia. Despite these concerns, Abdifatah reiterated that the government was confident in the national army's ability to assume greater security responsibilities as Ugandan and other foreign troops gradually withdraw. somalia.summary: The Somali federal government has dismissed fears of a security vacuum following the withdrawal of Ugandan troops, asserting that the Somali National Army (SNA) is ready to take over their positions. Information Minister Abdifatah Qasim Mohamud emphasized that the government has invested significantly in training and strengthening its armed forces in recent years. He noted that Ugandan troops have already begun handing over some positions to Somali forces as part of a planned security transition. Despite concerns from some lawmakers about the SNA's readiness, Abdifatah argued that Somalia must not remain reliant on foreign troops for security. He highlighted the SNA's role in liberating areas from the militant group al-Shabab, countering claims that the country is unprepared for the transition. While international officials have raised concerns about potential vulnerabilities, the Somali government remains confident in its military's capacity to manage security as foreign forces withdraw.

somalia.title: Somali Airlines sets Dec. 10 relaunch date after 35 years of inactivity - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Somali Airlines sets Dec. 10 relaunch date after 35 years of inactivity - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somali Airlines sets Dec. 10 relaunch date after 35 years of inactivity 11 Shares Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday November 24, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somalia's national carrier, Somali Airlines, is scheduled to relaunch on Dec. 10, 2026, after more than 35 years of inactivity, Transport and Civil Aviation Minister Mohamed Farah Nuh announced Monday. Speaking to reporters in Mogadishu on Nov. 23, Nuh said preparations were underway and that an official launch ceremony would be held next month to mark the return of the state-owned airline. advertisements “Somali Airlines is returning this coming December, and its official launch will take place then,” the minister said. The announcement follows years of government pledges to revive the airline, which ceased operations in 1991 after the collapse of Somalia's central government. Successive administrations have announced plans to restore the carrier, but previous launch dates have passed without commercial flights resuming. In July 2025, the Somali government announced an agreement to acquire two Airbus A320 aircraft as part of preparations to restart the airline. Officials initially said operations would begin within two months. The Transport Ministry later announced plans to resume operations before the end of 2025, but the airline did not return to service. In August 2026, Somali Civil Aviation Authority Director General Ahmed Moallin Hassan said preparations were nearing completion and that the first flights were expected in September. That deadline also passed without commercial operations beginning. The latest announcement comes as reports indicate that Somali Airlines has arranged to lease a Dash 8-400 turboprop aircraft from Daallo Airlines, a private carrier operating in the region. However, neither the government nor the airlines have publicly provided full details of the leasing arrangement or confirmed whether the aircraft will operate the first scheduled flights. The government has also not announced the airline's initial destinations, ticket prices or the date when passengers will be able to book flights. It remains unclear whether the Dec. 10 ceremony will coincide with the start of commercial passenger services or serve as an official inauguration ahead of operations. Established in 1964, Somali Airlines previously operated domestic and international flights connecting Mogadishu with destinations in Africa, the Middle East and Europe. The airline suspended operations following the outbreak of civil war in 1991, leaving Somalia without an operational national flag carrier for more than three decades. The proposed relaunch is part of the federal government's efforts to rebuild national infrastructure and strengthen air transport connections with regional and international markets. However, the repeated postponements have raised questions about whether the latest deadline will mark the carrier's return to commercial service. Somali aviation authorities have not yet published a confirmed flight schedule or provided a detailed timetable for the airline's full operational launch. The airline, which ceased operations in 1991 due to the civil war, has faced multiple delays in its revival despite government promises. Preparations for the relaunch are reportedly underway, with an official ceremony planned for next month. The government previously announced plans to acquire two Airbus A320 aircraft and has now arranged to lease a Dash 8-400 turboprop from Daallo Airlines. However, details regarding initial destinations, ticket prices, and the start of commercial flights remain unclear. The relaunch is part of broader efforts by the federal government to rebuild national infrastructure and enhance air transport connections. Despite the optimism surrounding the announcement, skepticism persists due to past postponements of the airline's return to service.
