somalia.content: Ghost strikes: the new drone superpowers raining death from above | Somalia | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation Print subscriptions Newsletters Sign in US US edition UK edition Australia edition Europe edition International edition The Guardian - Back to home The Guardian News Opinion Sport Culture Lifestyle Show more Hide expanded menu News View all News US news US politics Midterms 2026 World news Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness Opinion View all Opinion The Guardian view Columnists Letters Opinion videos Cartoons Sport View all Sport Soccer NFL Tennis MLB MLS NBA WNBA NHL F1 Golf Culture View all Culture Film Books Music Art & design TV & radio Stage Classical Games Design a better world Lifestyle View all Lifestyle The Filter Wellness Fashion Food Recipes Love & sex Home & garden Health & fitness Family Travel Money Search input google-search Search Support us Print subscriptions Newsletters Download the app Digital Archive Guardian Licensing Live events About Us The Guardian app Video Podcasts Pictures Inside the Guardian Guardian Weekly Crosswords Puzzles & games Corrections Tips Search input google-search Search Digital Archive Guardian Licensing Live events About Us Warning: contains graphic content some readers may find upsetting Scroll to continue “Parts of my body were still wet, and when I looked around as I lay on the ground, I realised this was from the blood of my family,” he says. “Saynab’s head was severed from the rest of her body. My children were unrecognisable. Their bodies were very burned and black, ripped to pieces.” Still, as he lost consciousness again, he was sure who they were. “I knew they were my daughters, because the body parts strewn out in the cave were so small.” Rights and freedom Somalia Ghost strikes: the new drone superpowers raining death from above The spread of cheap drones means warfare is increasingly conducted by invisible armies at the push of a button. Victims have no warning and no chance for justice Supported by About this content By Tess McClure and Mohamed Gabobe . Graphics by Ana Lucía González Paz , Prina Shah and Garry Blight Wed 25 Nov 2026 01.00 EST Last modified on Wed 25 Nov 2026 13.50 EST Share Death had come from the sky for Mohamed’s family: an execution carried out with no warning, no trial, no guilty verdict or chance for recourse. He did not even know who had carried out the killing, or under which authority – several nations have drones patrolling the skies of Somalia looking for Islamic State militants, including the US, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Turkey and the Somali government. Any one of them could have pulled the trigger. In Somalia, locals call these “ghost strikes” because the killer remains a phantom. With so many drones dropping bombs , and so many states (as well as non-state groups) operating their own drones, those being bombed may have little idea of who is killing them or precisely why. Few countries publish data on where they carry out drone strikes, and even this is incomplete. Often, the only clues come from scattered fragments of bomb casings left behind, or what can be deduced from who is operating in the area or might have enemies there. The phenomenon is a problem in countries far beyond Somalia. Ghost strikes reflect a fundamental shift in the way people conduct warfare. The machinery of war once required presence: soldiers on the ground or in the cockpit, tanks rolling through the streets, barracks and flags and bases. Only a small number of countries had the equipment – long-distance missiles and air forces – required to carry out a remote war, and those were relatively easy to monitor. Because most armies were physically present, there was also a stronger possibility of gathering evidence and holding them to account when it went terribly wrong: civilians massacred or war crimes committed. Now, as cheap drones proliferate and become more accessible, thousands of civilians are being killed by remote control , at vast distances, sometimes by operators from countries with no boots on the ground at all. In Sudan’s brutal civil war, drones have rapidly overtaken ground troops as the leading cause of civilian death this year . Most often, no party takes responsibility for a strike. Last month, dozens of civilians were killed in strikes in Tigray, where Tigrayan, Ethiopian and Eritrean forces are all using drones – no one has claimed credit for the strikes or deaths. Chart showing the main countries supplying armed drones to African countries On the Horn of Africa – which includes Somalia, Ethiopia and Sudan – the problem is playing out at a grand scale , with at least 11 nations or militant groups operating military drones in those three countries. But we are seeing the same thing in multiparty conflicts across the world, including Yemen, Iran, Myanmar and elsewhere. Chart showing how fatalities linked to drone use in conflict increased from 2,281 in 2024 to 9,079 in 2026 According to new data from Drone Wars , more than 55 countries are now operating large, armed, predator-style drones, with seven other states due to acquire them soon. Chris Cole, director of Drone Wars, says this number is probably a significant undercount – the dataset doesn’t include the far cheaper one-way kamikaze models that detonate on impact, and there is nothing forcing countries or companies to announce when they have bought or sold drones, so many more could be acquiring them covertly. Map showing how the number of countries acquiring Male drones has increased from 2001, and especially in Africa from 2024 Drones have also become stunningly cheap, in warfare terms. A US fighter jet costs between $80m (£66m) and $300m – amounts that once ensured air supremacy was the preserve of rich countries and centralised governments. But low-cost drones manufactured in Turkey and China are transforming the market, and creating a new set of drone superpowers. A Turkish-made medium altitude long endurance (Male) drone, which can conduct long-distance flights, is equipped with infrared cameras, stays airborne for more than 24 hours and carries more than about 130kg or 300lb of explosives, costs between $2m and $5m for each unit. Since Turkey began introducing cheap predator-style military drones in the mid-2010s, followed by China in the 2020s, they have become new “drone superpowers” transforming the market and equipping dozens of new countries for air wars. Simpler drones, especially the kamikaze units, can now be bought for as little as $200, with hundreds of new drone startups entering the market, driven partly by the demand of the Russia-Ukraine war. The lower entry cost is shifting the balance of power in conflicts, inviting new players into air wars – even non-state actors including terrorist groups, militias and drug cartels are increasingly acquiring armed drones. It is also making it far harder to track who is killing who. “The more they proliferate, the more state and non-state actors lay their hands on these cheap drones, the more it makes accountability then really, really difficult,” says Abdullahi Halakhe, an expert on security in the Horn of Africa and Great Lakes region. “This is now one of the biggest problems for civilian protection.” Chart showing the cumulative number of non-state armed groups that are deploying drone strikes For Mohamed to learn who had killed his family on 21 May, it would require identifying the bomb fragments, tracing them back to the country of manufacture and finding out who had bought them. First, however, he had to survive. Mobile reception is limited in the Golis mountains, and he knew the nearest mobile phone mast was 3 miles (5km) away. The only way to find help was to drag himself in that direction. It was about noon when Abdullahi Omar, a resident in the nearby coastal town of Buruc, received a phone call saying something had happened in the mountains. The call came in from a nomad outside Baxaya who had come across Mohamed, terribly injured, at a river not far from the cave. Immediately, Omar began organising a team of men to go out and investigate. “We prepared 36 men in town to go out to Baxaya,” he says. double quotation mark Everyone who was picking up the body parts and wrapping up the remains had the sense that the same planes who massacred this family were now watching us. The group of men trekked about 19 miles, leaving Buruc during afternoon prayers and walking through the night to reach the site of the strike the following morning. Among those who volunteered for the long hike through the mountains was Mohamed Hassan. “When we finally made it to Baxaya we came across the dead family and injured man,” he says. “There were no Daesh [Islamic State] fighters anywhere, only the bodies of women and children.” The Golis mountains have been the centre of a global war against the Islamic State in Somalia, with the US carrying out hundreds of airstrikes in the region . The UAE has carried out strikes in the area, but does not publish any data on how many. And Turkey and Somalia’s governments are both also using Bayraktar drones for strikes in Somalia, but publish such minimal data that it is difficult to confirm exactly when or where. Baxaya, where Mohamed and his family were hit, was supposedly designated a “safe zone” by the Puntland regional government – which was confirmed by Somalia’s deputy ambassador to Tanzania, Ashkir Nuur, who represents the constituency. “The Puntland authorities have not apologised nor compensated the sole survivor. It happened under their jurisdiction but the sole survivor is yet to receive answers,” Nuur says. Local people say there were no Islamic State fighters nearby, and Male drone systems are equipped with sensitive, infrared camera systems for monitoring targets that should make it easy to distinguish a fighting force from a family with young children and 250 goats. Who, then, carried out the strike? The men gathered up the pieces of Mohamed’s children, wrapping them in cloth for burial. As they worked, they heard the insect moan of drones above. “While collecting the body parts of the family members, we could hear loud engines of planes – we couldn’t see them but could hear,” Hassan says. “Everyone who was picking up the body parts and wrapping up the remains had the sense that the same planes who massacred this family were now watching us.” The men worked as quickly as they could. They took a series of photos and videos to document the strike’s aftermath, showing the bodies of Seynab, Fadumo, Aman and Anab, and the strewn bodies of dead goats. Photographs and video of the strike site taken by these first responders and reviewed by the Guardian confirm Mohamed’s description of events, including the catastrophic blast injuries to his wife, her unborn child, their three daughters, and the subsequent explosion that killed hundreds of his goats. The Guardian is not publishing these images due to their graphic nature. In a video from the scene, one man stands before the four wrapped bodies, after they have been prepared for burial, and says: “The missile massacred the people right here, and as you have been told, these are their bodies. We want the world to watch this and know.” Among the drying blood and debris, the men found something else: the shattered pieces of two missile casings, lying in the dirt. With no country claiming responsibility for the strike on the family, these dusty chunks of metal would provide the only evidence trail between the family who died, their killers and the booming, multibillion-dollar industry that provided the equipment. Independent munitions experts Trevor Ball and NR Jenzen-Jones, of Armament Research services, have analysed the images of bomb fragments left at the scene for the Guardian and concluded that they are from a MAM-series munition, manufactured by the Turkish state-owned defence manufacturer Roketsan. Jenzen-Jones says the “bomb remnants pictured probably evidence a strike by an unmanned aerial vehicle [UAV], mostly likely a Bayraktar TB2”. Graphic showing the elements that allowed experts to conclude the fragments were consisten with an armed-drone strike The drone is named for its creator – Selçuk Bayraktar, one of the stars of Turkey’s drone industry. His company, Baykar, has had a meteoric rise since it brought the first Bayraktar drone on to the global market in 2014, and works closely with state-owned defence companies, arming its drones with Rokestan munitions. In 2016, Bayraktar married Sümeyye Erdoğan, the daughter of the president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, in a lavish wedding ceremony, drawing Baykar into even closer connection with its government. Turkey is a relatively recent entrant to the drone market, but it has rapidly dominated sales to new states buying large, predator-style drones – particularly across African and Arab countries. On the back of its drone manufacturers, the country’s entire defence export market has boomed, reaching more than £7.5bn last year , up more than 500% from a decade earlier . The country now claims to control 65% of the global drone market , and Baykar has become one of the world’s biggest military drone companies. This year, the country’s military exports are tracking toward a new record high. At the same time, Turkey has developed a reputation for relatively lax “no questions asked” export rules. A large portion of the governments that Turkey has sold drones to in the past five years are classed as fully authoritarian regimes (including Mali, Azerbaijan, Kyrgyzstan, Rwanda, Turkmenistan, Qatar, Uzbekistan, Chad, Togo, Niger, Tunisia, Djibouti, Burkina Faso, Kuwait, Libya, Somalia) and/or already embroiled in civil war or armed internal conflict (including but not limited to Sudan, Ethiopia, Nigeria, Somalia) . Numerous states on Turkey’s customer list have subsequently been accused of mass killings of civilians using their equipment. For Ankara, however, the explosion of the drone market has been a geopolitical success – with Turkey leveraging drone sales to massively grow its overseas political and military influence. A Turkish diplomatic representative said: “Turkish UAV exports to Sudan or Somalia, like those to other countries, are subject to guarantees that they will be used in full compliance with international law. There is no verified information indicating that Turkish-manufactured UAVs have been used in violation of the relevant international norms and regulations by the Sudanese Army or in Somalia.” Chart showing how 66% of Turkish armed Male drones go to authoritarian countries, 15.65% to hybrid authoritarian countries, and 18.75% to democratic countries Even tracing the missile that killed Mohamed’s family to its source, however, does not tell us who was responsible for pulling the trigger. The UAE, Turkey and the Somali government all fly Bayraktar drones in Somali skies. The US has also carried out hundreds of strikes in the region, but using its own drones. The Turkish, Somali and UAE governments did not respond to requests for comment on who dropped the bomb on Mohamed and his family. Here, the trail runs cold. Seynab, Aman, Anab and Fadumo’s killers remain ghosts. Hours after they arrived, the men began the long trek back through the mountains toward the coast. Hassan was one of those who carried Mohamed, hauling his body over the difficult, rocky terrain of the mountains for more than 24 hours. The whole way, the sound of planes followed them. “It would go away, then once again the noise would return, so we knew our every step was being watched,” Hassan says. “We were scared because we knew what the planes did to Mohamed and his family … They were innocent people, who did nothing wrong and were massacred by these same planes now hovering above us.” From Buruc, the company sent Mohamed on a raft to Bosaso, the nearest equipped hospital, for treatment. Before Mohamed had even arrived at the hospital, Abdulkadir Koudah, a family member, had heard the news and contacted local security services to inform them that a man who was the sole survivor of an airstrike was on his way. In the months since, “they haven’t helped us or given us any answers on who bombed the family”, he says. Mohamed is slowly recovering, although the wounds are still visible on his body. Still, he says: “The burns on my body are nothing compared to what my daughters went through. “They were excited about having another sibling and so was their mother, but everything changed in the blink of an eye and I don’t know who to blame.” Illustrations by Anagh Banerjee, graphics by Heidi Wilson Explore more on these topics Somalia Rights and freedom Turkey China Drones (military) Africa Middle East and north Africa Conflict and arms Share Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development News Opinion Sport Culture Lifestyle Original reporting and incisive analysis, direct from the Guardian every morning Sign up for our email About us Help Complaints & corrections Contact us Tip us off SecureDrop Privacy policy Cookie policy Tax strategy Terms & conditions All topics All writers Newsletters Digital newspaper archive Bluesky Facebook Instagram LinkedIn Threads TikTok YouTube Advertise with us Guardian Labs Work with us Accessibility settings Back to top © 2026 Guardian News & Media Limited or its affiliated companies. somalia.summary: The rise of drone warfare, particularly in Somalia, has led to a phenomenon known as "ghost strikes," where victims are killed from the sky without warning or accountability. Various nations, including the US, UAE, Turkey, and Somalia, operate drones in the region, targeting suspected militants but often resulting in civilian casualties. The lack of transparency surrounding these strikes complicates efforts to identify responsible parties, as many countries do not disclose their drone operations. The proliferation of affordable drones has enabled both state and non-state actors to engage in remote warfare, increasing civilian deaths and making accountability difficult. In Somalia, a recent incident highlighted this issue when a family was killed in a drone strike, with no clear indication of who was responsible. As drone technology becomes more accessible, the landscape of warfare is shifting, raising significant concerns about civilian protection and the ethical implications of remote combat.

Photo: ©YPN-OCHA/ Ahmed Haleem. # Yemen UN Relief Chief in Yemen to push for access, funding and release of detained aid workers The Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher arrived in Aden, Yemen this morning. Mr. Fletcher’s visit focuses on four priorities: expressing solidarity with Yemen’s civilian population; advocating for increased funding to sustain humanitarian operations; calling for the immediate and unconditional release of detained UN personnel and other humanitarians; and pressing for safe and sustained humanitarian access, particularly in Ta’iz. Warning that severe underfunding is pushing the humanitarian response to the breaking point, Mr. Fletcher calls for greater international support and reaffirms the UN’s commitment to keeping Yemen high on the global humanitarian agenda. # Sudan Deadly drone strikes intensify as aid response remains underfunded OCHA is deeply concerned by the escalation of hostilities in Blue Nile State in Sudan, which has reportedly resulted in civilian deaths and injuries. Yesterday, local sources reported a wave of drone strikes targeting several locations across Blue Nile State, including Ed Damazine, the state capital, and Ar Rusayris town immediately to the north. The strikes reportedly killed 17 civilians in Ed Damazine and injured several others. Through the Sudan Humanitarian Fund , OCHA has allocated nearly US$36 million to humanitarian partners this year to support health, nutrition, cash assistance, shelter, protection, water, sanitation and hygiene interventions, among others, in Blue Nile State. However, very significant gaps remain and additional funding is urgently needed to continue to scale up the response as the situation deteriorates further. The UN reminds all parties to the conflict that civilians and civilian infrastructure must never be targeted and are protected under international humanitarian law. The UN also renews its call for all sides to facilitate immediate, safe and sustained humanitarian access. # Occupied Palestinian Territory Gaza: Meningitis cases rise as water, sanitation crisis deepens The UN and humanitarian partners reiterate that shortages of engine oil, lubricants, spare parts and maintenance equipment in Gaza are hampering aid operations and disrupting essential services. Water and sanitation partners report that less than half of the solid waste collection machinery operated by service providers is operational. The water trucking fleet of private desalination operators has fallen from 500 to 150 trucks. Desalination plants are also operating below capacity because of shortages of water treatment chemicals and generator shutdowns. Against this backdrop, communicable diseases are on the rise. Yesterday, the World Health Organization (WHO) reported more than 533 meningitis cases and four associated deaths. Cases rose rapidly in mid- and late October, mostly affecting children under one year of age. Overall, Gaza's Ministry of Health has reported 15 meningitis-related deaths since the start of 2026. The Ministry linked this rise in cases to worsening living and environmental conditions. These include overcrowding, damaged water and sewage networks, possible contamination of drinking water and poor hygiene conditions. Limited laboratory capacity is making it harder to distinguish between viral and bacterial meningitis. This is delaying efforts to provide a targeted response. WHO is working with the Ministry of Health and water and sanitation partners to expand disease surveillance, strengthen laboratory capacity and put protocols for treating patients into practice. WHO is also calling for the unimpeded entry of medical supplies to respond to disease outbreaks. West Bank: Demolitions leave Palestinian community empty In the West Bank, OCHA reports that last Sunday, Israeli authorities demolished all 44 remaining structures in the Palestinian community of Khirbet Samra, in Tubas governorate in the Jordan Valley. The demolitions displaced the last two households living there — 19 people, including seven children. The demolitions also affected essential infrastructure and assets that support livelihoods. These included animal shelters, fodder storage facilities, water tanks, latrines and solar power systems. The community is now empty following the successive waves of displacement linked to settler violence and demolitions. So far this year, 1,567 people in the Jordan Valley have been displaced due to settler violence, related access restrictions and demolitions due to lack of Israeli-issued building permits. That is nearly one third of the around 5,000 people displaced in total. The UN reiterates that Palestinians across the Occupied Palestinian Territory must be protected, as required by international law. Perpetrators of violations must be held accountable. # Somalia Funding crisis forces closure of nutrition sites, cuts health services OCHA warns that millions of people in Somalia are approaching the end of the year without the assistance they need, as the UN and humanitarian partners have been forced to scale back operations, mainly due to funding shortfalls and access constraints. With just weeks left in the year, the $852 million Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan is only 36 per cent funded, with $306 million received. This has severely constrained operations and partners’ ability to reach people in need. Between January and October, the UN and its humanitarian partners reached some 920,000 people with lifesaving assistance. However, this is just 38 per cent of the more than 2.4 million people targeted under the response plan. This means more than 1.5 million people have not yet been reached. Food assistance has fallen sharply. The number of people receiving support dropped from slightly above 1.1 million in January to 600,000 in June, and to an average of about 411,500 people per month between July and September. Nutrition and health services have also been affected. At least 233 nutrition sites have closed across the country, while services have been scaled back at 380 health facilities and mobile teams, reducing access to essential care. Additional funding is urgently needed to sustain remaining humanitarian operations and prevent further cuts to vital services. Without it, even more people will be at risk of going without critical assistance. somalia.summary: The UN's Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) highlights urgent humanitarian crises in Yemen, Sudan, the Occupied Palestinian Territory, and Somalia. In Yemen, UN Relief Chief Tom Fletcher emphasizes the need for increased funding and safe access for aid, as the humanitarian response faces severe underfunding. In Sudan, escalating drone strikes in Blue Nile State have resulted in civilian casualties, with OCHA calling for immediate humanitarian access and additional funding to support affected populations. In the Occupied Palestinian Territory, deteriorating conditions in Gaza have led to a rise in meningitis cases, exacerbated by water and sanitation shortages. Meanwhile, in the West Bank, demolitions have displaced families and destroyed essential infrastructure. In Somalia, a funding crisis has forced the closure of nutrition sites and cut health services, leaving millions without necessary assistance. OCHA warns that without urgent funding, the humanitarian situation will worsen significantly across these regions.

somalia.title: Somalia, Uganda agree to strengthen security cooperation against al-Shabab - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Somalia, Uganda agree to strengthen security cooperation against al-Shabab - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia, Uganda agree to strengthen security cooperation against al-Shabab Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday November 24, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni have called for intensified military operations against al-Shabab and alternative funding arrangements to sustain Ugandan troops deployed in Somalia, as uncertainty grows over the future of African Union peacekeeping operations. In a joint communiqué issued Monday, Nov. 23, following talks in Entebbe, Uganda, the two leaders emphasized the need for adequate, predictable and sustainable funding for the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) and closer military cooperation to combat the al-Qaeda-linked militant group. advertisements The discussions came during Hassan Sheikh's one-day official visit to Uganda at Museveni's invitation, as Kampala begins a phased withdrawal of troops deployed under bilateral security arrangements with Somalia. The two presidents called on AUSSOM and the Somali National Armed Forces to increase offensive operations against al-Shabab while exploring alternative financing mechanisms for forces operating under bilateral agreements. They also urged closer coordination among countries contributing troops to the African Union mission to strengthen counterterrorism operations and preserve security gains achieved over nearly two decades. The leaders praised the contributions of the Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF), Somali troops and other African Union peacekeepers, paying tribute to soldiers killed or wounded during operations against al-Shabab. They reaffirmed their commitment to consolidating security gains achieved under AUSSOM and its predecessor missions, the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (ATMIS) and the African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM). The presidents also referred to decisions reached during an extraordinary summit of AUSSOM troop-contributing countries held in Kampala on July 31, where leaders called for a coordinated security transition and sustained international financial assistance. Uganda, one of the largest contributors to African Union military operations in Somalia since 2007, began withdrawing troops deployed under bilateral arrangements earlier this month. The Ugandan military has also announced plans for a gradual withdrawal of its AUSSOM contingent by the end of 2027, raising concerns about potential security gaps in areas previously protected by its forces. However, Monday's communiqué did not announce any changes to Uganda's withdrawal timetable or confirm whether additional funding had been secured. Beyond military cooperation, Hassan Sheikh and Museveni emphasized the importance of political reconciliation and cooperation between Somalia's federal government, federal member states and other stakeholders. The leaders called for stronger relations through dialogue, good governance and peacebuilding to support security, stability and economic development. Their appeal comes as Somalia faces political disagreements over constitutional amendments, the mandates of federal institutions and the timetable for national elections. Opposition groups and the administrations of Puntland and Jubaland have rejected constitutional changes extending presidential and parliamentary terms, calling for a negotiated political settlement. The federal government maintains that the amendments provide a legal basis for elections scheduled in 2027. The joint communiqué did not announce any mediation initiative or specific agreement to resolve the political dispute. The two presidents also reviewed progress in bilateral economic cooperation, welcoming agreements and decisions reached during the Somalia-Uganda Joint Business Forum and Exhibition held in Mogadishu from Oct. 20 to 22. They welcomed the signing of a bilateral labor agreement and the agreed terms for a Bilateral Air Services Agreement aimed at expanding economic cooperation and transportation links. The leaders also revisited a proposal discussed during Hassan Sheikh's previous visit to Uganda on Oct. 26 to establish a warehouse in Mogadishu for Ugandan commercial goods. They agreed to continue considering the development of a port facility to facilitate trade and investment between the two countries. The proposals are intended to improve the movement of goods and expand commercial opportunities as Somalia and Uganda strengthen their economic partnership. Both leaders reaffirmed their commitment to regional integration through the East African Community, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development, the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa and the African Union. They also called on international partners to continue supporting Somalia's security institutions, humanitarian response and efforts to address climate change. The presidents welcomed logistical and operational assistance provided by the United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS), which supports African Union peacekeeping operations and Somali security forces. At the conclusion of the visit, Hassan Sheikh invited Museveni to visit Somalia. The Ugandan president accepted the invitation, with the dates to be arranged through diplomatic channels. The joint communiqué was signed in Entebbe by Somalia's Foreign Minister Abdisalam Abdi Ali and Ugandan Foreign Minister Adonia Ayebare. somalia.summary: Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni have agreed to enhance military cooperation against the al-Shabab militant group during a recent meeting in Entebbe, Uganda. They emphasized the need for intensified military operations and sustainable funding for the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), especially as Uganda begins a phased withdrawal of its troops. The leaders called for increased offensive actions by AUSSOM and the Somali National Armed Forces while exploring alternative financing for military operations. They also highlighted the importance of political reconciliation within Somalia amid ongoing disputes over constitutional amendments and election timelines. Additionally, the two presidents discussed strengthening economic ties, including a bilateral labor agreement and potential trade facilitation projects. They reaffirmed their commitment to regional integration and called for continued international support for Somalia's security and humanitarian efforts. The meeting concluded with an invitation for Museveni to visit Somalia, which he accepted. (158 words)

somalia.title: Ethiopia’s Strategic Recalibration Concurrent with Uganda’s Withdrawal from Somalia - horn review
somalia.content: Ethiopia’s Strategic Recalibration Concurrent with Uganda’s Withdrawal from Somalia – HORN REVIEW Home Research and Analysis Ethiopia and the World Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Publications Horn Review Journal Articles Policy Briefs The Greater Horn: Monthly Strategic Brief Horn Review Magazine Weekly Geopolitical Report Research Paper Commentary Event Flagship Events Conferences Brainstorming Sessions Team About Us Contact Us Search Home Research and Analysis Ethiopia and the World Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Publications Horn Review Journal Articles Policy Briefs The Greater Horn: Monthly Strategic Brief Horn Review Magazine Weekly Geopolitical Report Research Paper Commentary Event Flagship Events Conferences Brainstorming Sessions Team About Us Contact Us 2026-11-25 Ethiopia’s Strategic Recalibration Concurrent with Uganda’s Withdrawal from Somalia 0 Comments Uganda’s phased withdrawal from Somalia announced in late October 2026 and set for completion by the end of 2027 shows a structural shift in the Horn of Africa’s security. For nearly two decades Ugandan forces have formed a central pillar of the African Union’s efforts in the country, first under AMISOM and later under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia. Their departure which includes both bilateral contingents and those serving under the AU framework creates an immediate security space at a moment of acute political fragmentation in Mogadishu. For Ethiopia this is a clarifying moment that requires disciplined recalibration of military posture, alliance order and the defense of core national interests along the shared border. Uganda has long secured sensitive installations in and around Mogadishu including the presidential palace and the international airport. Its drawdown from positions in Lower Shabelle and related sectors removes a physical shield just as Somalia’s federal government confronts an unresolved political crisis. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s term expired in May 2026 and disagreements over electoral modalities have deepened tensions between the federal center and opposition actors as well as with several regional administrations. Into this space Al Shabaab stands to regain operational freedom along key approaches to the capital. Somali national forces still consolidating capacity are not yet positioned to fill the gap fully or rapidly. Mogadishu’s most probable response is heavier reliance on Turkish air and drone capabilities together with contributions from other partners including Egyptian forces operating under or alongside the AUSSOM framework. Turkey has invested substantially in Somalia through training facilities, infrastructure and hydrocarbon exploration. Reports indicate prospective resources in Somali offshore blocks with estimates of substantial reserves under active survey and drilling arrangements. Egypt’s involvement while framed as stabilization support is viewed by administrations in Puntland, Jubaland and South West State as an external presence that risks aggravating internal political fault lines. The resulting activities could intensify centrifugal pressures rather than contain them. Parallel constraints affect the broader mission with AUSSOM’s logistics backbone has facing uncertainty linked to decisions on United Nations Support Office in Somalia funding. Earlier notifications pointed toward reduced or terminated support around the end of 2026 with subsequent adjustments extending limited windows. Without reliable sustainment of fuel, medical services, transport and related enablers the operational viability of the roughly 12,000 strong mission becomes constrained. Continuing large scale Ethiopian deployments under a framework whose long term financing remains unresolved would present an inefficient use of national resources. A more coherent Ethiopian approach centers on two complementary tracks. The first is a measured reduction of force levels under AUSSOM accompanied by the consolidation of a resilient bilateral defense zone along the Ethiopian and Somali border. This zone extending approximately 100 to 150 kilometers inside Somali territory from the Dollo Ado area toward Ferfer and encompassing key localities in Gedo, Bakool and the approaches to Baidoa would serve multiple purposes. It would deny Al Shabaab the ability to use the borderlands as a staging ground for cross border operations. It would establish a clear geographic buffer that limits the westward projection of any external forces toward Ethiopian territory. And it would enable Ethiopia to shape security outcomes in southern Somalia from a position of geographic advantage rather than through open ended commitment to a financially strained multilateral mission. The second track involves deeper, direct security and economic engagement with regional administrations that share practical interests in containing Al Shabaab and managing the risks of excessive centralization. South West State, Jubaland and Puntland have demonstrated both capacity and willingness to function as autonomous partners on security matters. Strengthening these relationships reduces the leverage that any single federal configuration in Mogadishu might attempt to exercise and anchors Ethiopian influence in durable local realities. Uganda’s reported reorientation toward closer ties with Abu Dhabi adds a further diplomatic opening. Kampala’s evolving external partnerships create space for practical coordination among Ethiopia, Uganda and the United Arab Emirates on intelligence sharing, logistics and maritime access. The UAE’s established positions in Berbera and Bossaso offer complementary depth that can reinforce landward security arrangements. Such coordination need not take the form of a rigid alliance it can function as a flexible mechanism among actors with converging interests in regional stability and the prevention of exclusive spheres of influence. Ankara’s hydrocarbon exploration and infrastructure projects depend on a baseline of security that has historically benefited from broader regional military contributions. As Ethiopian forces consolidate closer to the border and reduce exposure in central Somalia the security environment around key assets will adjust. This creates natural incentives for dialogue. Turkey has every reason to seek predictable arrangements that protect its interests and Ethiopia is well placed to engage on the basis of mutual recognition of security requirements rather than open ended subsidy of external political preferences. The central error to avoid is the continued commitment of Ethiopian manpower and resources to sustain a political and security order in Mogadishu that yields diminishing returns for national defense while serving the strategic math of others. Parking forces under an AUSSOM framework whose sustainment is uncertain would constitute precisely such a misallocation. The alternative consolidating a defensible cross border zone cultivating practical partnerships with regional administrations and leveraging Ethiopia’s indispensable geographic and military position is not disengagement. It is the reassertion of agency. Uganda’s departure is frequently described as a loss for the African Union mission. For Ethiopia it is more accurately understood as a moment of clarity. The era of open ended subsidized security provision is drawing to a close. What replaces it will be shaped by those actors prepared to define their interests with precision defend them with credible capacity and negotiate from positions of strength. Ethiopia possesses the geography, the military capability and the historical stake required to influence that outcome. Acting with discipline and focus on national security priorities will determine whether the transition strengthens or erodes Ethiopia’s long term position in the Horn. somalia.summary: Ethiopia is undergoing a strategic recalibration in response to Uganda's planned withdrawal from Somalia, which is set to conclude by the end of 2027. Uganda has been a crucial player in the African Union's military efforts in Somalia for nearly two decades, and its exit creates a security vacuum amid political instability in Mogadishu. This situation presents Ethiopia with an opportunity to reassess its military posture and alliances, particularly along its border with Somalia. The Ethiopian strategy involves reducing its forces under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission (AUSSOM) while establishing a defensive zone within Somalia to counter Al Shabaab and limit external influences. Additionally, Ethiopia aims to strengthen ties with regional administrations like South West State and Jubaland, fostering local partnerships to enhance security. Uganda's shift towards closer relations with the UAE may also facilitate regional coordination on security matters. Ethiopia's ability to navigate this transition effectively will be crucial for its long-term stability and influence in the Horn of Africa.

somalia.title: Somalia-Türkiye ties built on development, not interference: defence minister Fiqi - TRT Afrika
somalia.content: Somalia-Türkiye ties built on development, not interference: defence minister Fiqi - TRT Afrika | English | English POLITICS AFRICA TÜRKİYE OPINION FEATURES SPORTS AFRICA 5 min read Somalia-Türkiye ties built on development, not interference: defence minister Fiqi Relations between Mogadishu and Ankara is based on tangible achievements and not activities that undermine Somalia’s stability, says Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi. Share Somalia's Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi praised relations with Türkiye. / Other By Nuri Aden Somalia’s outgoing Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi has praised the country’s deepening strategic partnership with Türkiye. The minister said that relations between Mogadishu and Ankara are built on development, reconstruction and tangible achievements and not foreign interference or activities that undermine Somalia’s stability. Fiqi made the remarks during the inauguration of a Turkish-backed school and the laying of the foundation stone for a new hospital in Warsheikh, a coastal district in Somalia’s Middle Shabelle region, where Türkiye is also constructing a major spaceport. “The relationship between Türkiye and Somalia goes much deeper than some people think. We have become intertwined and closely connected. No one can separate us,” Fiqi said. He described the partnership as one rooted in practical cooperation, pointing to Turkish involvement in Somalia’s infrastructure, defence, education, healthcare and emerging space technology sectors. “Our friendship is based on these achievements. It is not based on destruction, it is not based on interference and it is not based on bringing enemies into our country,” Fiqi said. The minister also criticised what he described as plots and activities intended to undermine Somalia, contrasting them with Türkiye’s contribution to the country’s reconstruction. Turkish-backed development projects Fiqi said the newly inaugurated school in Warsheikh had been rebuilt and refurbished with modern facilities, including solar power, classroom equipment, textbooks, schoolbags and other educational supplies. “The people of Warsheikh are very fortunate,” he said, noting that the district was benefiting from educational and healthcare projects needed in other parts of the country. The projects follow an October visit to Warsheikh by Türkiye’s Ambassador to Somalia, Ferhat Alkan, his first official trip outside Mogadishu since taking up his diplomatic post. Alkan later met Warsheikh District Commissioner Mohamed Hassan Mataan to discuss Turkish-supported development initiatives, including the renovated school and additional buildings for the district hospital. The two officials also discussed plans to establish a community kitchen providing food to vulnerable residents and an orphanage to support children in need. The initiatives form part of expanding Turkish engagement in Warsheikh, which has attracted growing attention because of its role in Türkiye’s plans to establish a satellite and rocket launch facility on Somalia’s Indian Ocean coast. Warsheikh emerges as centre of Türkiye’s space ambitions RECOMMENDED Multiple fatalities reported in fuel tanker fire in Egypt's Giza Nigeria arrests five Mexicans in $227m meth-lab bust Kenyan cult leader convicted of new charges after killing 190 children Ebola mourners say unable to locate bodies of relatives RECOMMENDED Multiple fatalities reported in fuel tanker fire in Egypt's Giza Nigeria arrests five Mexicans in $227m meth-lab bust Kenyan cult leader convicted of new charges after killing 190 children Ebola mourners say unable to locate bodies of relatives Beyond education and healthcare, Warsheikh is becoming a strategic location for Türkiye’s space programme, with construction under way on a spaceport designed to support future satellite launches and space research. During his October visit, Ambassador Alkan toured the project site alongside Major General Sebahattin Kalkan, commander of the Somalia–Turkish Task Force (TURKSOM). The delegation received a briefing on construction progress from Ahmet Sami İşler, Albayrak Group’s general manager in Somalia and chairman of the Türkiye–Somalia Business Council under Türkiye’s Foreign Economic Relations Board (DEİK). Turkish officials have presented the project as a major step towards developing independent satellite launch capabilities and expanding technological cooperation with Somalia. “With this project, Somalia will become one of the world’s leading centres in the field of space studies and activities,” the Turkish Embassy said. The facility is being developed as part of Türkiye’s national space programme, taking advantage of Somalia’s geographical position near the equator and its access to the Indian Ocean, which offers favourable conditions for launching spacecraft. Türkiye’s Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacır announced in December 2025 that feasibility and design studies had been completed and the first phase of construction had begun. Turkish authorities have said the planned spaceport could eventually support domestic satellite launches and provide services to international commercial operators. The project could also create opportunities for Somalia in technological training, scientific research and skilled employment. For Warsheikh, the spaceport represents another dimension of expanding Turkish investment in an area where Ankara is also supporting education, healthcare and community infrastructure. Expanding defence and strategic cooperation Fiqi said the successive projects demonstrated the breadth of relations between Somalia and Türkiye, citing Ankara’s involvement in Mogadishu’s international airport, seaport and military development. He also recalled a ceremony held days earlier in Mogadishu for the construction of facilities intended to strengthen the Somali Navy, including a naval command headquarters. Türkiye has become one of Somalia’s principal strategic partners, providing military training, defence assistance and support for public infrastructure. Ankara operates a major military training academy in Mogadishu, where Turkish officials have trained Somali personnel as part of efforts to rebuild the country’s armed forces. The two governments signed a 10-year defence and economic cooperation agreement in 2024, expanding cooperation in maritime security and the development of Somalia’s naval capabilities. Fiqi thanked the Turkish government, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Türkiye’s diplomatic and military representatives in Somalia and Turkish defence company Baykar for their contributions. “We thank them all and extend our deepest appreciation,” he said. His remarks came shortly after Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre appointed Saadaq Omar Mohamed Hassan as Somalia’s new defence minister, ending Fiqi’s tenure at the ministry, which began in April 2025. Opinion November 25, 2026 Updated: November 25, 2026 Greater Somalia Is a Failed Political Dream Respect the Will of the People November 25, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin Telegram Viber Farah Maalim Mohamed (MP) Political Contradictions, Historical Realities And The Responsibility Of Political Speech Eng. Abdi Ali Barkhad Political Analyst, Writer Senior Consultant It is increasingly difficult to take seriously the political arguments of Farah Maalim Mohamed, a veteran Kenyan Parliament member, politician, lawyer and public commentator who frequently speaks about Somalia, Somaliland, Ethiopia and the wider Horn of Africa. A man who has spent decades in public life and presents himself as an experienced political voice should be expected to demonstrate consistency, intellectual discipline, historical understanding and a sense of responsibility in his public statements. Unfortunately, some of his recent arguments raise serious questions about the consistency, credibility and realism of his political reasoning. For more than 25 years, I have followed many of his interviews, political discussions and public commentaries on Somali affairs and the Horn of Africa. When one looks back at many of his statements and political positions over the years, one cannot help but notice a pattern of changing narratives, political contradictions and arguments that sometimes appear to shift according to the political circumstances. Political experience alone does not necessarily translate into political wisdom, and speaking frequently about regional affairs does not automatically make one’s arguments credible or constructive. Two days ago, 0n 21Nevember 2026, I listened to an interview he gave to Dhaanka TV, in which he discussed Somalia, Somaliland, Ethiopia and the broader political situation in the Horn of Africa. What particularly caught my attention was his argument concerning Somaliland’s statehood, Farah Maalim should acknowledge that Somaliland’s statehood was not achieved through political gifts, goodwill, or the generosity of others. It was regained through enormous sacrifices, bloodshed, financial resources, years of struggle, and the unwavering determination of its people to restore their sovereignty and dignity. It is therefore deeply contradictory and irresponsible for Farah Maalim, while discussing Somaliland, to suggest that it should be brought back into Somalia by force if it refuses to accept integration with the Somali Federal Government. Such rhetoric disregards the history, sacrifices, and political will of the people of Somaliland. This is where his argument becomes politically contradictory, intellectually questionable and disconnected from the realities of the Horn of Africa. How can a politician deny the enormous human cost of Somaliland’s political struggle and, at the same time, advocate a strategy that could expose other Somali communities to further conflict, destruction and bloodshed? Does he genuinely believe that the political challenges of the Horn of Africa can be resolved through force, territorial ambitions and emotionally charged political rhetoric? Or is he simply making statements that sound politically attractive to certain audiences without adequately considering their practical implications, political consequences or human cost? The history of Somaliland cannot be reduced to political fantasies or rewritten according to the ambitions and preferences of individual politicians. Somaliland’s experience in 1960, its subsequent union with Somalia, the devastating consequences of the late 1980s and its reassertion of independence in 1991 constitute a significant historical and political journey. These realities deserve serious analysis, not simplistic political arguments or speculative strategies. If Farah Maalim acknowledges that Somaliland’s statehood has involved enormous sacrifices, then he should equally understand the importance of peace, political stability and the consequences of advocating approaches that could potentially lead to further conflict. It is neither intellectually consistent nor politically responsible to recognise the sacrifices of one community while promoting political rhetoric that could expose other communities to similar suffering. Farah Maalim should understand that political commentary is not a substitute for political strategy, and rhetoric is not a substitute for leadership. Making bold statements on television does not necessarily demonstrate political wisdom, intellectual depth or a genuine understanding of the realities facing the region. I have deliberately refrained from responding to many of his statements over the years, and several people have advised me not to engage in unnecessary political arguments. Nevertheless, his latest remarks deserve a direct response and a sincere piece of advice. Farah Maalim, you are an older man, an experienced politician and a lawyer who has spent decades in public life. At this stage of your political career, it is time to demonstrate the wisdom, intellectual consistency and political responsibility that should accompany such experience. Political maturity requires more than making provocative statements or promoting ambitions without a credible, peaceful and realistic framework. The Horn of Africa has suffered enough from wars, political miscalculations, divisive rhetoric and irresponsible leadership. The region does not need politicians who repeatedly promote territorial ambitions and historical grievances without offering realistic and peaceful solutions. It needs diplomatic engagement, intellectual honesty, responsible leadership, respect for historical realities and a genuine commitment to peace and stability. My advice to you is straightforward: think carefully before you speak. Your political experience should be reflected in the quality, consistency and wisdom of your arguments. At this stage of your career, it would be far more constructive to contribute to peace, political understanding and realistic solutions than to continue making statements that neither advance the interests of the Somali people nor offer a credible path forward. A politician’s legacy is not determined by how frequently he appears on television, how loudly he speaks or how ambitious his political statements sound. It is determined by the wisdom of his positions, the consistency of his arguments and the positive contribution he makes to the political future of his people and the region. The future should not be dictated by force, nostalgia, or political rhetoric, but by the will of the people, peaceful coexistence, mutual respect, and dialogue. The time has come to move beyond the political dream of Greater Somalia and respect the realities and aspirations of the people wherever they live. It argues that Maalim's recent comments, suggesting that Somaliland should be forcibly integrated into Somalia, disregard the historical sacrifices made by the people of Somaliland in their quest for independence. السوداني الدوري السوداني الممتاز المريخ الهلال السوداني الأهلي مروي كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin عاش الشارع السوداني اليوم الأربعاء 25 نوفمبر، أجواء احتفالية بمناسبة افتتاح النسخة الـ31 من مسابقة الدوري السوداني الممتاز، التي شهدت حدثًا غير مسبوق بإقامة 8 مباريات في يوم واحد. وشهدت ملاعب 9 مدن سودانية منافسات قوية وسط حضور جماهيري كبير، تحدى الظروف الاقتصادية الطاحنة وغياب أبسط مقومات الحياة الكريمة جراء تداعيات الحرب المدمرة التي اندلعت في منتصف أبريل 2023؛ لتختلط مشاعر الفرح بالعودة التدريجية للحياة إلى طبيعتها. إقبال جماهيري كبير في يوم افتتاح الدوري السوداني وسجلت العاصمة وشمال السودان حضورًا جماهيريًا لافتًا، حيث افتتح رئيس اتحاد الكرة السوداني، معتصم جعفر سر الختم، البطولة من ملعب الخرطوم بمباراة المريخ وكوبر، بحضور وزير الشباب والرياضة الاتحادي أحمد آدم. كما أُقيمت مراسم احتفالية على ملعب مدينة كريمة الذي احتضن لقاء الهلال حامل اللقب والأهلي مروي. وبعيدًا عن انتصار قطبي الكرة السودانية، حققت البطولة في يومها الأول نجاحًا جماهيريًا كبيرًا عكس رغبة كبيرة في إنجاحها رغم تحديات الأزمة الاقتصادية الطاحنة، والانتقادات الموجهة لاتحاد الكرة بسبب التسرع في تنظيم المسابقة دون توفير البيئة الملائمة للأندية، ما أثار تذمر عدد منها. واستهل المريخ مشواره بانتصارٍ عريضٍ قوامه 4-0 على نظيره كوبر، في مباراةٍ شهدت تألقًا لافتًا للعديد من النجوم الشباب، بينما تعكرت الأجواء بإصابةٍ مقلقةٍ لقائد الفريق "البحراوي" الطاهر سادومبا، حالت دون إكماله اللقاء. اقرأ أيضا المريخ يضرب بقوة محليًا وخارجيًا في يوم الانطلاق المثالي الهلال يستهل حملة الدفاع عن لقبه بفوز ثمين بالدوري السوداني وفي مدينة كريمة شمالي البلاد، احتفى نجوم الهلال مع جماهيرهم في مشهدٍ يعكس الدور الكبير لوجود بطل الدوري في إعادة الحيوية للمدينة. وشهد افتتاح النسخة 31 من مسابقة الدوري السوداني الممتاز حدثًا غريبًا تمثل في غياب فريق الأمير عن مواجهة الفلاح لعدم وصوله إلى مدينة عطبرة، مما أثار قلقًا حول تنظيم football.summary: استهل فريق الهلال السوداني حملة الدفاع عن لقبه بفوز ثمين على الأهلي مروي بنتيجة 1-0 في الجولة الأولى من الدوري السوداني الممتاز، التي أقيمت على ملعب مدينة كريمة. سجل الهدف الوحيد للمباراة المحترف النيجيري أكيري تايو في الشوط الأول، مما يعكس جاهزية الهلال البدنية والفنية بعد معسكره التحضيري في كيغالي. المدرب الفرنسي ألكسندر لافيت، الذي تولى قيادة الفريق قبل ساعات من المباراة، حقق بداية مثالية في مسيرته مع الهلال، حيث اعتمد على مزيج من اللاعبين المخضرمين والشباب. يعتبر الهلال المرشح الأبرز لتصدر مجموعته والتأهل إلى المرحلة النهائية من الدوري، حيث سيواجه هلال كريمة في الجولة الثانية مطلع ديسمبر. هذا الفوز يعزز آمال جماهير الهلال في الاحتفاظ باللقب، ويعكس قوة الفريق في بداية الموسم.

المعاناة إلى المستطيل الأخضر.. الدوري السوداني يعود في نسخة تاريخية من مواجهة سابقة بين الهلال والمريخ في الدوري السوداني (winwin) 24 نوفمبر 2026 من رحم المعاناة إلى المستطيل الأخضر.. الدوري السوداني يعود في نسخة تاريخية الدوري السوداني الممتاز المريخ الهلال السوداني كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' يترقب الشارع السوداني انطلاق النسخة 31 من الدوري السوداني الممتاز، التي تفتتح يوم الأربعاء 25 نوفمبر في 9 ملاعب بمختلف ولايات البلاد، في حدثٍ تاريخي يشهد مشاركة 33 ناديًا، وهو رقم قياسي غير مسبوق في تاريخ البطولة. تعود الحياة إلى ملاعب الدوري في ظل ظروف استثنائية، تزامنا مع استقرار نسبي تشهده البلاد، وبوادر عودة النازحين الذين هجروا ديارهم قسرًا، هربًا من جحيم الحرب التي اندلعت في منتصف أبريل 2023، وذلك وسط تحديات جسيمة تواجه الأندية واتحاد الكرة لإنجاح المسابقة. 9 مواجهات قوية في اليوم الأول لانطلاق الدوري السوداني وتنطلق المنافسة بمواجهة المريخ لنظيره كوبر في العاصمة الخرطوم، بينما يستهل الهلال حملة الدفاع عن لقبه بملاقاة الأهلي مروي على ملعب مدينة كريمة الأولمبي. وفي بقية المباريات، يلتقي الفلاح عطبرة بضيفه الأمير دنقلا على ملعب عطبرة، ويستضيف دبروسة حلفا فريق المريخ بورتسودان، فيما يواجه الميرغني كسلا ضيفه الشرطة القضارف. كما يلتقي حي الوادي نيالا مع الفجر الأبيض على ملعب كوبر، ويستقبل الرابطة كوستي نظيره الأهلي مدني ، بينما يحتضن ملعب مدني مواجهة أم مغد ضد الشباب المناقل، ويستقبل المريخ الأبيض ضيفه الهلال المناقل. نسخة الأرقام القياسية حطمت النسخة 31 من مسابقة الدوري السوداني الممتاز أرقامًا قياسية، إذ تشهد مشاركة 33 ناديًا في رقم غير مسبوق في تاريخ المنافسة، كما تسجل 9 أندية ظهورها الأول، مما يبشر بسجالات تاريخية بالجملة. اقرأ أيضًا إدارة المريخ تزف بشرى سارة لجماهيرها رغم التعثر مهمة مزدوجة واستعانة عاجلة.. هكذا يبدأ لافيت رحلته مع الهلال وتستمر مشاركة المدرب برهان تيه؛ الذي كان حاضرا في النسخة الأولى التي انطلقت عام 1996، ليقود "عميد المدربين السودانيين" فريقه الأهلي مروي في مواجهة صعبة أمام الهلال، كما يعد المريخ والهلال الناديين الوحيدين اللذين احتفظا بمكانهما في المنافسة منذ انطلاقتها وحتى الآن. وتقام المسابقة هذا الموسم بنظام جديد يعتمد على تقسيم الأندية إلى 4 مجموعات، تتأهل منها 3 أندية عن كل مجموعة إلى "دوري النخبة"؛ وهي المرحلة الختامية التي تقام بنظام الدوري من دورة واحدة في العاصمة الخرطوم، بمشاركة 12 ناديا، ليتوج باللقب الفريق الأكثر حصدا للنقاط. النشرة البريدية اشترك معنا بالنشرة البريدية لتصلك آخر أخبار الرياضة اشترك معنا دول كرة القدم الأخبار الدوريات الفرق رياضات التنس كرة السلة رياضات ميكانيكية football.summary: تستعد السودان لإطلاق النسخة 31 من الدوري السوداني الممتاز، الذي سيبدأ في 25 نوفمبر 2026، بمشاركة قياسية تصل إلى 33 ناديًا، وهو رقم غير مسبوق في تاريخ البطولة. تأتي هذه النسخة بعد ظروف صعبة عاشتها البلاد، بما في ذلك النزاعات التي أدت إلى تهجير العديد من السكان. ومع ذلك، هناك بوادر أمل مع عودة النازحين واستقرار نسبي. ستشهد الجولة الأولى من الدوري مواجهات مثيرة، حيث يلتقي المريخ مع كوبر في الخرطوم، بينما يبدأ الهلال حملة الدفاع عن لقبه بمواجهة الأهلي مروي. تم اعتماد نظام جديد للمسابقة يقسم الأندية إلى أربع مجموعات، حيث يتأهل ثلاثة أندية من كل مجموعة إلى "دوري النخبة" النهائي. هذه النسخة تعد بمنافسات تاريخية، حيث تشارك تسعة أندية لأول مرة، مما يضفي طابعًا جديدًا على البطولة.

football.content: نجم المريخ السابق يكشف أبرز أزمات الدوري السوداني نجم المريخ السابق يكشف أبرز أزمات الدوري السوداني مباريات اليوم أحمد السيد نجم المريخ السابق والمدرب الحالي لفريق حي العرب بورتسودان (winwin) 24 نوفمبر 2026 نجم المريخ السابق يكشف أبرز أزمات الدوري السوداني الدوري السوداني الممتاز المريخ الهلال السوداني كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أعرب أحمد السيد الفاتح، نجم المريخ والمنتخب السوداني السابق ومدرب فريق حي العرب، عن ثقته في تقديم فريقه أداءً متميزًا في النسخة 31 من الدوري السوداني الممتاز والتي تنطلق يوم الأربعاء 25 نوفمبر/ تشرين الثاني، مسلطًا الضوء في الوقت ذاته على الأزمات والصعوبات التي تواجه فريقه وبقية أندية المنافسة. وفي حديث خاص لموقع "winwin"، رشح السيد مدرب النادي الذي تطلق عليه الجماهير لقب "السوكرتا"، قطبي الكرة السودانية المريخ والهلال للتتويج باللقب، موضحًا أسباب ذلك. كما أشاد بنظام المسابقة، متمنيًا أن تقام في ظروف ملائمة مستقبلًا، بما يبعث مؤشرًا إيجابيًا حول عودة الحياة الطبيعية إلى البلاد وتجاوز تداعيات الحرب التي اندلعت في عام 2023. مدرب المريخ السابق ينتقد التأجيل المتكرر للدوري وأكد مدرب "حي العرب بورتسودان" أنّ التأجيلات المتكررة للدوري أثرت سلبًا على جاهزية الأندية، قائلًا: "عدم استقرار اتحاد الكرة على موعد محدد للمنافسة تسبب في ارتباك واضح وتأخير في التحضيرات". وأضاف: "باستثناء المريخ و الهلال ، بدأت بقية الأندية إعدادها قبل فترة قصيرة من انطلاقة الموسم، كما أنّ سوء الملاعب يمثل أزمة حقيقية أخشى أن تلحق الضرر باللاعبين". اقرأ أيضًا تغييرات جذرية وتحديات مزدوجة.. المريخ يستعد لمرحلة جديدة ثورة مفاجئة في الهلال السوداني قبل بدء الدوري.. ما الأسباب؟ ورشح نجم المريخ ومدربه السابق عملاقي الكرة السودانية للتتويج بلقب الدوري، مستبعدًا دخول أي أندية أخرى دائرة المنافسة، حيث قال: "أعتقد أن المريخ والهلال مرشحان لمواصلة سيطرتهما على المسابقة بفضل إعدادهما الجيد وإمكانياتهما المالية الكبيرة بالمقارنة مع بقية الأندية"، مضيفًا: "قد يواجهان صعوبات نسبية في المراحل المتقدمة، لكن من الصعب أن يظفر غيرهما باللقب". ووصف قرار إدارة المريخ بإسناد مهمة التدريب للمدرب جندي نميري بالجريء، معلقًا: "اتخذت الإدارة قرارًا صائبًا بمنح الثقة للمدرب نميري؛ فهو مدرب قدير وأتمنى أن يجد الدعم اللازم. سيواجه اختبار الديربي الصعب في رواندا، وأثق في قدرته على تجاوزه. مباريات القمة دائمًا ما تكون خارج نطاق التوقعات ولا تخضع لحسابات مسبقة". كما تمنى النجاح للنسخة الجديدة من مسابقة الدوري الممتاز، متوقعًا أن يسهم الحضور الجماهيري في دعم البطولة، وأضاف: "أحسن اتحاد الكرة في اختيار نظام البطولة بتقسيم الأندية إلى مجموعات، مما يقلل الضغط في ظل وجود 33 ناديًا. أتمنى أن تحقق البطولة أهدافها وتدعم مشروع العودة الطوعية، كما آمل أن تعود الحياة إلى طبيعتها ويعم الأمن والأمان البلاد، لتتمكن البطولة من العودة لنظامها المعتاد في ظروف أفضل". أخبار ذات صلة الدوري السوداني الممتاز الدوري السوداني يشهد افتتاحًا استثنائيًا بـ8 مباريات 25 نوفمبر 2026 المريخ المريخ يضرب بقوة محليًا وخارجيًا في يوم الانطلاق المثالي 25 نوفمبر 2026 الهلال football.content: الهلال السوداني يستهدف تحقيق مهمة مزدوجة الهلال السوداني يستهدف تحقيق مهمة مزدوجة مباريات اليوم رياضات كرة القدم الأخبار فيديو البطولات البرامج دول الهلال السوداني يستهدف تحقيق مهمة مزدوجة من مباراة سابقة لفريق الهلال السوداني في الدوري الرواندي (Facebook/ Al Hilal S.C) 23 نوفمبر 2026 الهلال السوداني يستهدف تحقيق مهمة مزدوجة الهلال السوداني دوري أبطال أفريقيا الدوري السوداني الممتاز كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' يستعد فريق الهلال السوداني لخوض مواجهة قوية أمام نظيره كييفو سبورت الرواندي، يوم الثلاثاء 24 نوفمبر، على ملعب "كيغالي بيليه"، ضمن منافسات الجولة الخامسة المؤجلة من الدوري الرواندي. وقرر مدرب الفريق جوزيف زينباور خوض اللقاء بدلًا من تأجيله، ليجعله بروفة ختامية قبل مواجهة حوريا كوناكري الغيني يوم الأحد 29 نوفمبر على ملعب "أماهورو"، في افتتاح مشوار الفريق بدور المجموعات في دوري أبطال أفريقيا . تشكيل الهلال السوداني المتوقع ضد كييفو سبورت الرواندي من المتوقع أن يعتمد الألماني زينباور في مباراة الغد على تشكيلته الأساسية؛ للوقوف على جاهزية عناصره قبل التحدي القاري، لا سيما بعد إشراك وجوه جديدة أثبتت كفاءتها في الاختبار الأخير، مثل الموريتاني أحمد مختار، رغبة منه في تعزيز الانسجام بين اللاعبين بعد فترة التوقف الدولي التي أبعدتهم عن أجواء المنافسات الرسمية. ومن المتوقع أن يستعين زينباور بالعناصر التالية: حراسة المرمى: سفيان فريد خط الدفاع: مصطفى كرشوم، بابي ديارا، إرنست لوزولو، ياسر عوض خط الوسط: محمد راوا، ولي الدين خضر، عبد الرؤوف يعقوب خط الهجوم: أنسومانا سامورا، محمد عبد الرحمن، أحمد مختار اقرأ أيضًا ثورة مفاجئة في الهلال السوداني قبل بدء الدوري.. ما الأسباب؟ الهلال يخطف فوزًا ثمينًا من البوليس ويقترب من صدارة الدوري الرواندي ويعدّ مدرب الهلال السوداني الذي يقضي موسمه الأول مع النادي الأزرق، عددًا من البدلاء لتجهيزهم لماراثون المباريات الشاق الذي ينتظر الفريق، إذ سيخوض 3 مواجهات في المرحلة الأولى من مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا، بالتزامن مع منافسات قوية في الدوري الرواندي. ويطمح الفريق إلى تحقيق مكاسب مضاعفة من مباراته المقبلة، تتمثل في اعتلاء صدارة الدوري بنسخته الجديدة، ومنح نجومه دفعة معنوية كبيرة قبل خوض football.summary: يستعد فريق الهلال السوداني لمواجهة كييفو سبورت الرواندي يوم الثلاثاء 24 نوفمبر، في الجولة الخامسة المؤجلة من الدوري الرواندي، على ملعب "كيغالي بيليه". قرر المدرب جوزيف زينباور عدم تأجيل المباراة، معتبرًا إياها بروفة مهمة قبل مواجهة حوريا كوناكري الغيني في دوري أبطال أفريقيا يوم الأحد 29 نوفمبر. من المتوقع أن يعتمد زينباور على تشكيلته الأساسية لتعزيز الانسجام بين اللاعبين بعد فترة التوقف الدولي. يسعى الهلال لتحقيق مكاسب مزدوجة من هذه المباراة، تتمثل في اعتلاء صدارة الدوري الرواندي ومنح اللاعبين دفعة معنوية قبل المنافسات القارية. يواجه الفريق تحديات كبيرة هذا الموسم، حيث يسعى للاحتفاظ بلقب الدوري السوداني والوصول إلى نصف نهائي دوري أبطال أفريقيا. المباراة ستنطلق في الساعة 7:30 بتوقيت مكة المكرمة، وستُبث عبر منصات النادي الرسمية.
